evidence.effect: All models exceeded 90% MCQ accuracy, but clinical scenarios yielded low-scoring responses (Deepseek-V2.5 n=51) with hallucinations and omitted safety warnings.
evidence.quote: These discrepancies highlight a critical gap between knowledge possession and clinically reliable knowledge application, with direct implications for safe deployment.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical scenario questions (plus 103 multiple-choice questions; 7 questions in prompt phase)

evidence.title: Evaluating the quality of artificial intelligence responses to psoriasis-related clinical and patient questions: a comparative study of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy, evidence consistency, completeness and safety of chatbot psoriasis responses (max 8)
evidence.effect: Mean scores 7.36±0.97 (ChatGPT), 7.77±0.77 (Gemini), 7.05±1.09 (Copilot); differed significantly (Friedman P<0.001); all models showed high clinical safety but incomplete responses.
evidence.quote: The observation that models may provide accurate yet clinically incomplete responses, particularly for treatment content, emphasizes the need for physician oversight when AI-generated information is used in dermatological practice.

evidence.title: Comparative Performance of GPT-5 and Gemini Models in Decision Support for Bariatric Surgery: A Simulation-Based Study
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, safety, and guideline adherence of LLMs on bariatric surgery vignettes
evidence.effect: GPT-5 accuracy 87.3% vs Gemini 72.4%; guideline adherence 78% vs 46%; unsafe recommendations 2.1% vs 8.4%; unsafe outputs persisted.
evidence.quote: GPT-5 achieved higher accuracy (87.3% vs. 72.4%), stronger guideline adherence (78% vs. 46%), and fewer unsafe recommendations (2.1% vs. 8.4%).

evidence.title: Performance comparison of large language models for medication counseling in people living with HIV
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated quality of five LLMs on real-world HIV medication questions
evidence.effect: Composite scores: DeepSeek 4.47, Qwen 4.33, Kimi 4.24, Doubao 4.13, ChatGPT 3.41 (H=182.14, p<0.001); all models showed significant limitations on complex pharmaceutical inquiries.
evidence.quote: All models demonstrated significant limitations when handling complex pharmaceutical inquiries and cannot fully replace professional clinical pharmacists.

evidence.title: Blinded two-phase evaluation of large language models in complex cardiac surgery: task-specific performance and human-AI collaboration
evidence.outcome: Whether benchmark/exam performance predicts competence in complex clinical decision-making
evidence.effect: Top models scored well overall, but even O1 showed deficits in patient safety (0.600) and hallucination avoidance (0.667) on expert-designed scenarios.
evidence.quote: Our results highlight that strong performance by LLMs on standardized exams does not ensure safe or reliable application in complex, high-stakes clinical decision-making.
evidence.sample_unit: cardiac surgery scenarios (rated by 5 surgeons; 3,750 binary ratings)

evidence.title: Performance of multimodal Large Language Models in misdiagnosed dermatologic cases: a pilot study on diagnostic accuracy and human error replication
evidence.outcome: Multimodal LLM top-1 diagnostic accuracy on misdiagnosed dermatology cases
evidence.effect: Multimodal Top-1 accuracy: Gemini 3 60.0% (18/30), ChatGPT-5.2 56.7% (17/30), Claude 4.5 Sonnet 33.3% (10/30); limited accuracy for malignant lesions using macro-images.
evidence.quote: Gemini 3 achieved the highest multimodal Top-1 accuracy (60.0% (18/30), followed by ChatGPT-5.2 at 56.7% (17/30) and Claude 4.5 Sonnet at 33.3% (10/30).

evidence.title: When Wrong Answers Matter: Consequence-Weighted Evaluation of Large Language Models for ERCP Triage
evidence.outcome: LLM guideline-based ERCP triage accuracy and under-triage errors on synthetic vignettes
evidence.effect: Accuracy 96.0% GPT-5.5, 90.0% Gemini 3.0 Pro, 84.0% Claude 4 Opus; Claude produced 9 under-triage errors and 163.8 simulated delay hours per 100 vignettes (P = .007).
evidence.quote: Claude 4 Opus produced the most under-triage errors (n = 9) and the largest simulated delay burden (163.8 hours per 100 vignettes; Kruskal-Wallis P = .007).

evidence.title: Structured reasoning failures compromise LLM interpretation of clinical oncology notes
evidence.outcome: Whether endpoint accuracy masks reasoning failures in LLM oncology note interpretation
evidence.effect: Endpoint accuracy alone may mask clinically meaningful reasoning failures; GPT-5.1 had reduced error rates but retained structured failure patterns.
evidence.quote: Endpoint accuracy alone may mask clinically meaningful reasoning failures.

evidence.title: Can AI improve triage quality? A preliminary assessment of ChatGPT performance in evaluating triage decisions
evidence.outcome: GPT-4o agreement with expert reference on intended-use triage evaluation task
evidence.effect: Exact agreement 46%, kappa 0.243; better in high-complexity cases (kappa 0.313; F1 0.704), lower in moderate and low-complexity cases.
evidence.quote: Exact agreement between ChatGPT and expert assessments was found in 46% of cases.

evidence.title: Single-session agreement of ChatGPT and Gemini treatment recommendations with multidisciplinary tumor board decisions in thoracic oncology
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM treatment recommendations with tumor board decisions on real cases
evidence.effect: Overall agreement with MDTB decisions was 52.0% for ChatGPT and 56.9% for Gemini; lower in pulmonary masses without pathological diagnosis and pulmonary metastases.
evidence.quote: In this single-session evaluation, overall agreement with MDTB decisions was 52.0% for ChatGPT and 56.9% for Gemini.

evidence.title: Comparison of DeepSeek-V3.2 and ChatGPT-5.2 in the outpatient diagnosis and treatment of prostate cancer: a multicenter evaluation of application value and multilingual adaptability
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic and treatment reasoning quality on real prostate cancer cases, vs MDT consensus
evidence.effect: Comprehensive scores 4.20-4.40 of 5; both LLMs competent but did not surpass expert MDT; performance declined with disease stage, lowest in mCRPC.
evidence.quote: Both LLMs demonstrate competent assistance potential for PCa outpatient management but do not surpass expert MDT judgment.

evidence.title: Predictive accuracy of a general-purpose artificial intelligence model for cut-out following proximal femoral nailing
evidence.venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
evidence.outcome: General-purpose ChatGPT accuracy for predicting cut-out from radiographs and clinical data
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 68.0%, specificity 62.7%, PPV 4.5%, AUC 0.694; 360 false positives vs 8 false negatives; judged clinically insufficient.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT demonstrated limited, clinically insufficient accuracy for predicting cut-out following proximal femoral nailing, with a prohibitive false-positive burden and inverted calibration.

evidence.title: Accuracy and Readability of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Vascular Surgery Patients: A Specialist Based Evaluation Highlighting the Current Landscape of Safety Risks and Accessibility Gaps
evidence.venue: European journal of vascular and endovascular surgery : the official journal of the European Society for Vascular Surgery
evidence.outcome: Clinical appropriateness, accuracy, comprehensiveness of ChatGPT vascular surgery answers by specialists
evidence.effect: Only 7 of 16 (44%) judged clinically appropriate by all reviewers; 50% acceptable accuracy, 69% acceptable comprehensiveness; treatment answers only 25% appropriate.
evidence.quote: Among the 16 outputs, only seven (44%) were judged clinically appropriate by all reviewers; clarity was rated adequate in 81% of responses, whereas only 50% reached acceptable accuracy and 69% acceptable comprehensiveness.

evidence.title: Qualitative and Quantitative Assessment of Four Artificial Intelligence Systems for Nasal Deformity Analysis in Rhinoplasty
evidence.outcome: Chatbot MIRA sub-score agreement with expert surgeons on nasal deformity photographs
evidence.effect: All four models differed significantly from experts on MIRA sub-scores (p<0.05); Grok 2 worst (p<0.001); only Claude 3.7 matched total MIRA score; ChatGPT 4o 70% accuracy on nose type.
evidence.quote: Detailed analysis of MIRA sub-scores showed a significant difference between chatbots and experts across all models (p < 0.05), including Claude.

evidence.title: Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence based chatbots in reporting jaw lesions from multimodal radiographic images: A cross-sectional study
evidence.outcome: Chatbot lesion detection and correct diagnosis accuracy on jaw lesion images
evidence.effect: Manus CBCT 95% detected and correctly diagnosed; Gemini 2.5 Pro 80% detected, 56% correctly diagnosed; Copilot and Claude least accurate; significant differences between chatbots.
evidence.quote: Significant discrepancies exist among artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots regarding their diagnostic accuracy in reporting jaw lesions.

evidence.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Assess Distal Radius Fracture Stability?
evidence.outcome: Multimodal LLM agreement with surgeon consensus on fracture stability using radiographs
evidence.effect: Both models achieved overall accuracy 0.75 (95% CI, 0.56-0.94); ChatGPT moderate and Claude fair agreement; several criteria near chance and specificity limited.
evidence.quote: Performance across several criteria approached chance levels, and specificity was limited.

evidence.title: Stepwise Diagnostic Evaluation of Chinese Large Language Models: Comparative Study of Common and Rare Diseases
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of LLMs on common (COPD) versus rare (RP) disease vignettes
evidence.effect: LLMs had significantly higher accuracy for COPD than RP across all metrics (P<.001). RP MRR ranged 0.10-0.39 versus COPD 0.82-0.89; RP accuracy was lower and less stable.
evidence.quote: LLMs demonstrated significantly higher diagnostic accuracy for COPD compared to RP across all metrics (P<.001).

evidence.title: Performance of nine large language models on real-world polysomnography interpretation for obstructive sleep apnea: a multi-dimensional comparative analysis
evidence.venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy on real-world polysomnography reports versus expert consensus, by case complexity
evidence.effect: Fully correct diagnostic rates ranged from 75.0% to 86.3%; all models degraded on complex cases (11.8-25.7 percentage point decline); safety rates exceeded 88%.
evidence.quote: All models demonstrated significant performance degradation on complex cases (11.8-25.7 percentage point decline).

evidence.title: A Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Diagnostic Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models in Radiology (RadM-Bench): Evaluation Development and Validation
evidence.outcome: Model diagnostic score change from public teaching cases to real routine clinical cases
evidence.effect: Proprietary models declined from RadEdu to RealClin (O3 with images: 1.14 to 0.79); Chinese-centric open-source models improved (InternVL3-78B: 0.48 to 0.75). All models stayed below 1.5 on the 0-3 scale.
evidence.quote: Cross-dataset transfer diverged by model category: proprietary models declined from RadEdu to RealClin (eg, O3 with images: 1.14 to 0.79), whereas Chinese-centric open-source models improved (eg, InternVL3-78B: 0.48 to 0.75).

evidence.title: Critical Care-Specific vs General-Purpose Large Language Models in Emergency Intensive Care Unit Diagnosis: Single-Center Retrospective Paired Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of LLMs on real EICU clinical cases
evidence.effect: All models' top-1 accuracy stayed below 70%, with heterogeneous performance across core EICU diseases including sepsis, severe pneumonia, and gastrointestinal bleeding.
evidence.quote: Notably, all models' top-1 accuracy stayed below 70%, and stratified analysis revealed heterogeneous performance across core EICU diseases including sepsis, severe pneumonia, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

evidence.title: Large language models for lumbar spondylolisthesis detection: a multi-center pilot comparative radiographic accuracy study
evidence.venue: European journal of orthopaedic surgery & traumatology : orthopedie traumatologie
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy detecting spondylolisthesis on radiographs versus spine surgeon consensus
evidence.effect: GPT-5 sensitivity 67.5% vs GPT-4o 49.4%; accuracy 61.5% vs 55.5%; specificity 57.3% vs 59.8%; kappa 0.238 vs 0.091. Both limited compared to spine surgeons.
evidence.quote: With expert surgeon consensus set as ground truth, ChatGPT-5 outperformed ChatGPT-4o evidenced by higher sensitivity (67.5% vs. 49.4%) and overall accuracy (61.5% vs. 55.5%), with minor difference in specificity (57.3% vs. 59.8%).

evidence.title: The Role of Google Gemini in the Interpretation of Ovarian Lesions
evidence.outcome: Gemini accuracy interpreting ovarian ultrasound (O-RADS/IOTA) vs histopathology, rated by GQS
evidence.effect: Mean GQS 3; 6/10 normal ovaries mischaracterized as pathologic; 6/10 benign lesions assigned O-RADS 4-5; 3/10 malignant misclassified as benign (O-RADS 2), plus 1 borderline tumor misclassified.
evidence.quote: Critical inconsistencies including overdiagnosis and dangerous misclassification of malignancies indicate the need for specialized, domain-specific models with rigorous validation before clinical implementation.

evidence.title: AI Clinical Decision Making Compared with Fellowship-Trained Hand Surgeons: A Case-Based Study
evidence.outcome: Concordance of commercial LLM platforms with surgeon plurality on hand surgery vignettes, by case complexity
evidence.effect: All four platforms 100% concordant on easy cases; on complex cases Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3/5 (60%), ChatGPT-4 and Open Evidence 1/5 (20%). Overall 78% for Claude/Gemini, 56% for ChatGPT-4/Open Evidence.
evidence.quote: Performance diverged on complex cases: Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini each achieved concordance on 3 of 5 complex cases (60%), whereas ChatGPT-4 and Open Evidence each achieved concordance on 1 of 5 (20%).
evidence.sample_unit: clinical vignettes (answered by 15 hand surgeons and 4 AI platforms)

evidence.title: Discordance Between Textual Reasoning and Visual Interpretation in Large Language Models for Low Back Pain: Cross-Sectional Quantitative Evaluation and Exploratory Multimodal Stress Test
evidence.outcome: Multimodal LLM image interpretation performance versus textual accuracy on low back pain cases
evidence.effect: Text accuracy 88.4% (1605/1816), but in pure imaging tasks the average diagnostic score was poor, with models failing to identify core pathologies.
evidence.quote: In pure imaging tasks featuring complex but clinically representative pathologies, the average diagnostic score was poor, with models failing to identify core pathologies.
evidence.sample_unit: individual recommendations extracted from LLM responses to 25 low back pain questions (plus 5 multimodal stress-test cases)

evidence.title: Reproducibility of Mandibular Cortical Index Classification Among Dental Examiners and a Single Generative AI Platform: An Observer Agreement Study
evidence.outcome: Agreement of generative AI MCI classification with dentists on panoramic radiographs
evidence.effect: AI-dentist agreement was slight or lower (κ < 0.2) for every pairing, with 95% CIs including zero; two-level discrepancy (Class 1 vs Class 3) in 10-18% of cases.
evidence.quote: However, agreement between the AI and the dentists remained at "slight agreement" or lower (κ < 0.2) for every pairing, with 95% confidence intervals that included zero; no formal global hypothesis test was performed, and these individual interval estimates should not be interpreted as proof of the absence of agreement beyond chance.

evidence.title: Are artificial intelligence systems ready for pediatric surgical decision-making? A comparative evaluation of large language models versus pediatric surgeons
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on pediatric surgery scenario diagnosis, investigation, treatment decisions vs surgeon reference
evidence.effect: Claude 145/150 (Po=0.967); ChatGPT and Gemini 144/150 (0.960); DeepSeek-V3 0.913; Perplexity 0.873, significantly different from surgeon (p=0.004). Errors clustered in investigation and treatment.
evidence.quote: In the overall analysis, only Perplexity demonstrated a performance level significantly different from that of the pediatric surgeon (p = 0.004).

evidence.title: A two-stage evaluation of large language models for guideline-based Q&A and draft rehabilitation planning in stroke care
evidence.outcome: Clinician-rated correctness, completeness, safety of LLM stroke Q&A and rehabilitation plans, and accuracy on 100 questions
evidence.effect: Stage 1 accuracy: DeepSeek 91%, ChatGPT-o3 90%, Gemini 85%, ChatGPT-4o 83%. ChatGPT-o3 outperformed DeepSeek on plan generation across all five domains; Q&A comparable.
evidence.quote: In Stage 1, DeepSeek achieved the highest accuracy (91%), followed by ChatGPT-o3 (90%), Gemini (85%), and ChatGPT-4o (83%).
evidence.sample_unit: de-identified stroke cases (Stage 2b); also 100 questions in Stage 1 and 20 guideline-derived questions in Stage 2a

evidence.title: Exploratory benchmarking of AI-generated diet plans for inherited protein metabolism disorders: a simulation-based evaluation of nutritional accuracy and clinical safety
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM diet plans meet disease-specific metabolic targets versus general nutritional adequacy
evidence.effect: Both models produced generally acceptable overall nutrition but missed disease-specific targets in all three disorders; conventional adequacy measures were insufficient to judge clinical appropriateness.
evidence.quote: These findings demonstrated that conventional measures of nutritional adequacy alone were insufficient to determine the clinical appropriateness of AI-generated dietary plans for inherited protein metabolism disorders.
evidence.sample_unit: 3-day AI-generated dietary plans (3 disorders x 2 models)

evidence.title: Large Language Models in Perioperative Antithrombotic Management: A Blinded Scenario-Based Expert Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated LLM performance on perioperative antithrombotic scenarios across models
evidence.effect: Overall expert-rated performance differed across models (Friedman χ2 = 28.75, p < 0.001; Kendall's W = 0.096); greater variability in discontinuation timing, anesthesia choice and clinical reasoning.
evidence.quote: Although all models performed well in drug discontinuation decisions, greater variability was observed in discontinuation timing, anesthesia choice and clinical reasoning.

evidence.title: Large language models fail to reliably predict emergent catheterization laboratory activation from prehospital electrocardiograms
evidence.venue: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
evidence.outcome: Multimodal LLM diagnostic performance identifying ECGs warranting cath lab activation vs cardiology decisions
evidence.effect: Gemini sensitivity 95.3% but specificity 9.4%; ChatGPT and Claude sensitivity 68.1% and 67.2%, specificity 42.3% and 46.5%; ECG machine algorithm sensitivity 67.7%, specificity 64.2%.
evidence.quote: Multimodal LLM interpretation of prehospital ECGs demonstrated clinically unreliable performance for identifying ECGs warranting emergent cardiac catheterization laboratory activation when benchmarked against real-world cardiology activation decisions.

evidence.title: The Alignment Paradox of Medical Large Language Models in Infertility Care: Decoupling Algorithmic Improvement From Clinical Decision-Making Quality
evidence.outcome: Whether automatic field-level metrics predict expert-rated clinical quality of LLM infertility decision support
evidence.effect: GRPO had highest automatic performance (e.g., infertility type accuracy 92.57%), yet blinded experts rated SFT directionally higher on reasoning and feasibility; SFT chosen best in 51.2% vs GRPO 26.2%.
evidence.quote: Outcome-based metrics alone are insufficient proxies for clinical utility in ART decision support.

evidence.title: Beyond the Leaderboard: Rethinking Medical Benchmarks for Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Clinical fidelity and safety-oriented dimensions of 53 medical LLM benchmarks audited with MedCheck checklist
evidence.effect: Benchmarks show a profound disconnect from clinical practice, unmitigated data contamination risks, and systematic neglect of robustness and uncertainty awareness (no numeric rates in abstract).
evidence.quote: Our analysis uncovers widespread, systemic issues, including a profound disconnect from clinical practice, a crisis of data integrity due to unmitigated contamination risks, and a systematic neglect of safety-critical evaluation dimensions like model robustness and uncertainty awareness.

evidence.title: PrinciplismQA: A Philosophy-Grounded Approach to Assessing LLM-Human Clinical Medical Ethics Alignment
evidence.outcome: Gap between LLM knowledge accuracy and clinical ethical reasoning performance
evidence.effect: Models showed significant ethical reasoning gaps despite high knowledge accuracy; no numeric results in the provided text.
evidence.quote: Evaluating recent models reveals significant ethical reasoning gaps despite high knowledge accuracy, demonstrating that knowledge-oriented training does not ensure clinical ethical alignment.

evidence.title: The Knowledge-Reasoning Dissociation: Fundamental Limitations of LLMs in Clinical Natural Language Inference
evidence.outcome: LLM factual knowledge probe accuracy versus clinical trial reasoning task accuracy
evidence.effect: Mean GKMRV knowledge-probe accuracy was 0.918 while mean accuracy on main reasoning tasks was 0.25; output consistency across samples averaged 0.87.
evidence.quote: Models achieve near-ceiling GKMRV accuracy (mean accuracy 0.918) yet perform poorly on the main reasoning tasks (mean accuracy 0.25).

evidence.title: MedFact: Benchmarking the Fact-Checking Capabilities of Large Language Models on Chinese Medical Texts
evidence.outcome: LLM veracity classification and error localization on Chinese medical fact-checking benchmark
evidence.effect: Models often determine if text contains errors but struggle to localize them precisely; top performers fall short of human performance; over-criticism misidentifies correct information as erroneous.
evidence.quote: We evaluate 20 leading LLMs on veracity classification and error localization, and results show models often determine if text contains errors but struggle to localize them precisely, with top performers falling short of human performance.

evidence.title: Beyond Classification Accuracy: Neural-MedBench and the Need for Deeper Reasoning Benchmarks
evidence.outcome: VLM performance on reasoning-intensive neurology benchmark versus conventional datasets
evidence.effect: Sharp performance drop on Neural-MedBench compared with conventional datasets; reasoning failures rather than perceptual errors dominate model shortcomings. No numbers given in abstract.
evidence.quote: Through systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4o, Claude-4, and MedGemma, we observe a sharp performance drop compared to conventional datasets.

evidence.title: Radiology's Last Exam (RadLE): Benchmarking Frontier Multimodal AI Against Human Experts and a Taxonomy of Visual Reasoning Errors in Radiology
evidence.outcome: Frontier model diagnostic accuracy on difficult radiology cases versus radiologists
evidence.effect: Radiologists 83%, trainees 45%, best AI model (GPT-5) 30%; models fall far short of radiologists on challenging cases.
evidence.quote: Board-certified radiologists achieved the highest diagnostic accuracy (83%), outperforming trainees (45%) and all AI models (best performance shown by GPT-5: 30%).

evidence.title: Simulating Viva Voce Examinations to Evaluate Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic performance in multi-turn interactive reasoning versus single-turn benchmark-style vignettes
evidence.effect: LLMs competent diagnosing from well-described presentations, but performance degrades significantly in iterative diagnostic reasoning under uncertainty on VivaBench (1762 vignettes).
evidence.quote: While current LLMs demonstrate competence in diagnosing conditions from well-described clinical presentations, their performance degrades significantly when required to navigate iterative diagnostic reasoning under uncertainty in our evaluation.

evidence.title: ECG-LLM -- training and evaluation of domain-specific large language models for electrocardiography
evidence.outcome: Consistency of model rankings across benchmark, automatic, LLM-judge and human expert evaluations
evidence.effect: Finetuned Llama 3.1 70B led on multiple-choice and automatic metrics, ranked second to Claude 3.7 in LLM-as-a-judge, while human experts favored Claude 3.7 and RAG for complex queries.
evidence.quote: Our findings reveal substantial performance heterogeneity across evaluation methodologies, underscoring assessment complexity.

evidence.title: Can Large Language Models Function as Qualified Pediatricians? A Systematic Evaluation in Real-World Clinical Contexts
evidence.outcome: LLM performance on licensing-level exam questions versus more complex tasks
evidence.effect: Qwen3-235B-A22B achieved over 90% accuracy on licensing-level questions, but performance declined ~15% as task complexity increased, revealing limitations in complex reasoning.
evidence.quote: State-of-the-art models performed well on foundational knowledge, with Qwen3-235B-A22B achieving over 90% accuracy on licensing-level questions, but performance declined ~15% as task complexity increased, revealing limitations in complex reasoning.

evidence.title: Generalist Foundation Models Are Not Clinical Enough for Hospital Operations
evidence.outcome: Zero-shot foundation model AUROC on real EHR-derived hospital operations tasks versus benchmark strength
evidence.effect: Zero-shot general-purpose and specialized models underperformed on four of five tasks (36.6%-71.7% AUROC); mortality prediction was the exception.
evidence.quote: In zero-shot settings, both general-purpose and specialized models underperform on four of five tasks (36.6%-71.7% AUROC), with mortality prediction being an exception.

evidence.title: NeuroABench: A Multimodal Evaluation Benchmark for Neurosurgical Anatomy Identification
evidence.outcome: MLLM accuracy on neurosurgical anatomical structure identification benchmark
evidence.effect: Best-performing MLLM achieved only 40.87% accuracy in anatomical identification; best of four trainees scored 56%, lowest 28%, average 46.5%.
evidence.quote: Experiments on over 10 state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal significant limitations, with the best-performing model achieving only 40.87% accuracy in anatomical identification tasks.
evidence.sample_unit: annotated neurosurgical video clips/questions (9 hours of video, 89 procedures, 68 anatomical structures)

evidence.title: The Illusion of Clinical Reasoning: A Benchmark Reveals the Pervasive Gap in Vision-Language Models for Clinical Competency
evidence.outcome: Gap between structured multiple-choice exam-style accuracy and open-ended multimodal clinical task accuracy
evidence.effect: Accuracy exceeded 90% on structured multiple-choice questions but scarcely reached 60% on open-ended tasks requiring multimodal integration.
evidence.quote: While state-of-the-art models achieved high accuracy, exceeding 90%, on structured multiple-choice questions, their performance markedly declined on open-ended tasks requiring multimodal integration, with accuracy scarcely reaching 60%.

evidence.title: MLB: A Scenario-Driven Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Clinical Applications
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on scenario-based clinical tasks versus structured knowledge tasks
evidence.effect: Top model Kimi-K2-Instruct scored 77.3% overall and 87.8% on MedRU but only 61.3% in patient-facing SmartServ, showing a translational gap.
evidence.quote: Our comprehensive evaluation of 10 leading models reveals a critical translational gap: while the top-ranked model, Kimi-K2-Instruct (77.3% accuracy overall), excels in structured tasks like information extraction (87.8% accuracy in MedRU), performance plummets in patient-facing scenarios (61.3% in SmartServ).

evidence.title: MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs through Counterfactual Differential Diagnosis
evidence.outcome: LLM baseline accuracy versus Bias Trap Rate on counterfactual diagnosis cases
evidence.effect: Frontier models achieved high baseline accuracy but severe bias trap rates across 17 LLMs, so accuracy on standard medical benchmarks overstated clinical competence. No numbers in abstract.
evidence.quote: Extensive Evaluation of 17 LLMs shows frontier models achieve high baseline accuracy but severe bias trap rates.

evidence.title: Benchmarking Egocentric Clinical Intent Understanding Capability for Medical Multimodal Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: MLLM performance on egocentric clinical intent understanding benchmark incl. hallucination and sycophancy traps
evidence.effect: Current MLLMs struggle with egocentric intent due to over-reliance on global features, producing fabricated observations and uncritical acceptance of invalid instructions. No numeric results in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Experiments reveal current MLLMs struggle with egocentric intent due to over-reliance on global features, leading to fabricated observations and uncritical acceptance of invalid instructions.

evidence.title: MedConsultBench: A Full-Cycle, Fine-Grained, Process-Aware Benchmark for Medical Consultation Agents
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy versus information-gathering efficiency and medication safety in consultation agents
evidence.effect: Across 19 LLMs, high diagnostic accuracy often masks significant deficiencies in information-gathering efficiency and medication safety, indicating a gap between medical knowledge and clinical practice ability.
evidence.quote: Systematic evaluation of 19 large language models reveals that high diagnostic accuracy often masks significant deficiencies in information-gathering efficiency and medication safety.

evidence.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Action Gap by Evaluating LLMs in Dynamic Dental Clinical Scenarios
evidence.outcome: Gap between static knowledge-task performance and dynamic simulated clinical dialogue performance
evidence.effect: Models show high proficiency in static objective tasks, but performance drops in dynamic multi-turn clinical dialogues. The bottleneck is active information gathering and dynamic state tracking.
evidence.quote: Our analysis reveals that while models demonstrate high proficiency in static objective tasks, their performance precipitates in dynamic clinical dialogues, identifying that the primary bottleneck lies not in knowledge retention, but in the critical challenges of active information gathering and dynamic state tracking.

evidence.title: Overalignment in Frontier LLMs: An Empirical Study of Sycophantic Behaviour in Healthcare
evidence.outcome: Whether benchmark accuracy predicts clinical reliability under sycophancy pressure
evidence.effect: Reasoning-optimized Thinking models show high vanilla accuracy but rationalize incorrect user suggestions under authoritative pressure; benchmark performance is not a proxy for clinical reliability.
evidence.quote: Our results across frontier models suggest that benchmark performance is not a proxy for clinical reliability, and that simplified reasoning structures may offer superior robustness against expert-driven sycophancy.

evidence.title: LiveMedBench: A Contamination-Free Medical Benchmark for LLMs with Automated Rubric Evaluation
evidence.outcome: LLM performance on contamination-free, real-world open-ended clinical cases versus inflated static benchmarks
evidence.effect: Best model achieved only 39.2%; 84% of models showed performance degradation on post-cutoff cases, indicating data contamination inflating static benchmark estimates.
evidence.quote: Extensive evaluation of 38 LLMs reveals that even the best-performing model achieves only 39.2%, and 84% of models exhibit performance degradation on post-cutoff cases, confirming pervasive data contamination risks.

evidence.title: ADRD-Bench: A Preliminary LLM Benchmark for Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias
evidence.outcome: Gap between high benchmark accuracy and reasoning quality/stability in caregiving case studies
evidence.effect: Top-tier models exceeded 0.9 accuracy, yet case studies showed inconsistent reasoning quality and stability, indicating benchmark accuracy overstates domain competence.
evidence.quote: While top-tier models achieved high accuracies (>0.9), case studies revealed inconsistent reasoning quality and stability, highlighting a critical need for domain-specific improvement to enhance LLMs' knowledge and reasoning grounded in daily caregiving data.

evidence.title: LiveClin: A Live Clinical Benchmark without Leakage
evidence.outcome: LLM performance on realistic clinical-pathway cases versus inflated static benchmark scores
evidence.effect: Top-performing model reached Case Accuracy of just 35.7% on 1,407 real case reports, and static benchmarks are described as giving inflated scores.
evidence.quote: Our evaluation of 26 models on LiveClin reveals the profound difficulty of these real-world scenarios, with the top-performing model achieving a Case Accuracy of just 35.7%.

evidence.title: RAG-X: Systematic Diagnosis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Question Answering
evidence.outcome: Gap between perceived accuracy and evidence-based grounding in medical RAG QA benchmarks
evidence.effect: Reveals an 'Accuracy Fallacy' in which a 14% gap separates perceived system success from evidence-based grounding.
evidence.quote: Our experiments reveal an ``Accuracy Fallacy", where a 14\% gap separates perceived system success from evidence-based grounding.

evidence.title: ThReadMed-QA: A Multi-Turn Medical Dialogue Benchmark from Real Patient Questions
evidence.outcome: Fully-correct response rate of LLMs on real patient multi-turn questions versus physician ground truth
evidence.effect: Even the strongest model, GPT-5, achieved only 41.2% fully-correct responses; all five models degraded significantly from turn 0 to turn 2 (p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: Even the strongest model, GPT-5, achieves only 41.2% fully-correct responses.

evidence.title: Stop Listening to Me! How Multi-turn Conversations Can Degrade LLM Reliability
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and abstention of LLMs in multi-turn conversations versus static clinical benchmarks
evidence.effect: Partitioning the answer space into sequential presentations reduced end-to-end accuracy and abstention against incorrect suggestions by an average of up to 30%, reaching 65% in certain models.
evidence.quote: Together our findings demonstrate that the general proficiency captured by static benchmarks do not translate over multi-turn dialogues.
evidence.sample_unit: LLMs evaluated across three clinical benchmarks

evidence.title: QuarkMedBench: A Real-World Scenario Driven Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Gap between exam-based scores and performance on real-world medical queries
evidence.effect: Baseline evaluations reveal significant performance disparities among state-of-the-art models on real-world clinical nuances; no numeric gap is reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Crucially, baseline evaluations on this benchmark reveal significant performance disparities among state-of-the-art models when navigating real-world clinical nuances, highlighting the limitations of conventional exam-based metrics.

evidence.title: The Validity Gap in Health AI Evaluation: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Benchmark Composition
evidence.outcome: Clinical composition of health LLM benchmarks versus real-world needs
evidence.effect: Benchmarks lack raw clinical artifacts: laboratory values 5.2%, imaging 3.8%, raw medical records 0.6%; chronic disease management only 5.5%; benchmark composition misaligned with real-world clinical needs.
evidence.quote: Evaluation benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world clinical needs, lacking raw clinical artifacts, adequate representation of vulnerable populations, and longitudinal chronic care scenarios.

evidence.title: Active Evidence-Seeking and Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models for Clinical Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy and evidence quality, multi-turn evidence seeking versus static full-context evaluation
evidence.effect: Multi-turn evidence seeking reduced diagnostic accuracy by 12.75% and supporting-evidence quality by 24.36% relative to full-context evaluation across 468 cases and 15 models.
evidence.quote: Together, these results suggest that static full-context benchmarks may overestimate performance in interactive evidence-seeking settings, motivating complementary interactive assessment for safer clinical decision support.

evidence.title: When Correct Beliefs Collapse: Epistemic Resilience of LLMs under Clinical Pressure
evidence.outcome: Gap between medical benchmark accuracy and belief robustness in clinical dialogue
evidence.effect: Despite strong medical benchmark accuracy, LLMs showed severe multi-turn sycophancy, abandoning initially correct diagnoses under escalating pressure.
evidence.quote: Despite strong medical benchmark accuracy, LLMs can exhibit severe multi-turn sycophancy in clinical dialogue, abandoning initial correct diagnosis under escalating pressure.

evidence.title: GlobalDentBench: A Multinational Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Clinical Reasoning in Dentistry with Expert Calibration
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy across question formats and reasoning levels on a dental benchmark
evidence.effect: Accuracy fell from 81.34% on multiple-choice to 64.53% on short-answer and 22.34% on case-based questions; from 74.01% at L1 to 55.64% at L2 and 35.71% at L3.
evidence.quote: Specifically, accuracy plummeted from 81.34% on multiple-choice to 64.53% on short-answer and 22.34% on case-based questions, while declining markedly from 74.01% at L1 to 55.64% at L2 and 35.71% at L3.

evidence.title: When Reasoning Hurts: Source-Aware Evaluation of Frontier LLMs for Clinical SOAP Note Generation
evidence.outcome: Whether reasoning benchmark gains transfer to SOAP note generation quality across three datasets
evidence.effect: Enabling reasoning significantly degraded GPT-5.4 performance across all three datasets; non-reasoning GPT-5.4 scored highest overall, so benchmark reasoning strength did not predict task quality.
evidence.quote: Overall, the findings indicate that stronger reasoning capability should not be assumed to improve fidelity-sensitive SOAP note generation without dedicated, task-specific evaluation.

evidence.title: Better Accuracies, Worse Reasoning: A Step-Level Audit of Medical Chain-of-Thought Distillation
evidence.outcome: Medical QA benchmark answer metrics versus step-level factuality of reasoning traces after CoT distillation
evidence.effect: MedQA-USMLE SC@64 rose 74.7% to 84.4% and ECE fell 0.096 to 0.034, while step error rate rose from 30.6% to 50.3% under an LLM-judge audit.
evidence.quote: Yet under a Kimi-K2.6 style-blind LLM-judge audit, its error rate over non-abstained steps rises from 30.6% to 50.3%.
evidence.sample_unit: reasoning steps (plus 150 steps in clinical expert audit)

evidence.title: MedCase-Structured: A Text-to-FHIR Dataset for Benchmarking Diagnostic Reasoning in Clinically Realistic EHR Settings
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy on structured FHIR inputs versus plain-text inputs
evidence.effect: LLMs showed consistently lower diagnostic accuracy on structured FHIR inputs than on plain text. Specific accuracy numbers are not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Evaluation on MedCase-Structured reveals consistently lower diagnostic accuracy for LLMs on structured FHIR inputs than with plain text, highlighting the importance of deployment-aligned benchmarking.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic FHIR bundles derived from clinician-authored diagnostic cases

evidence.title: CardioLens: Revealing the Clinical Reality Gap of MLLMs via Multi-Sequence Cardiac MRI Evaluations
evidence.outcome: MLLM performance on multi-sequence CMR image understanding, report generation, and diagnosis versus public benchmark performance
evidence.effect: Models perform poorly overall, with performance degrading along the real CMR workflow, despite strong performance on public medical benchmarks.
evidence.quote: Across 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs, CardioLens reveals a substantial clinical reality gap: models perform poorly overall, with performance degrading along the real CMR workflow.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Models in Dynamic Clinical Decision-Making with Standardized Patient Cases
evidence.outcome: Correlation of static benchmark performance with performance in interactive standardized patient scenarios
evidence.effect: Performance on static benchmarks does not reliably translate to SP scenarios; best model GPT-5.5 completes 60.4% of rubric items, best medical model 40.0%.
evidence.quote: Applying MedSP1000 to a range of general-purpose and medically specialized LLMs, we find that performance on static benchmarks does not reliably translate to such educational scenarios.

evidence.title: Stress-testing medical large language models reveals latent safety pathology beyond benchmark accuracy
evidence.outcome: Whether clean benchmark accuracy reflects safety under realistic stress
evidence.effect: Models were uniformly good on clean baseline but diverged sharply under narrative stress, so benchmark accuracy did not reveal safety-relevant failures.
evidence.quote: Under clean baseline conditions, all models performed uniformly well.

evidence.title: Reassessing High-Performing LLMs on Polish Medical Exams: True Competence or Bias-Driven Performance?
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy drop from standard MCQA to harder benchmark on Polish medical exams
evidence.effect: Best model (Qwen3.5-122B) drops 28.4 pp on English and 31 pp on Polish exams under the harder setup; standard MCQA scores do not reliably reflect true medical competence.
evidence.quote: Under our harder setup, the best model (Qwen3.5-122B) drops by 28.4 and 31 pp on English and Polish exams, respectively.

evidence.title: Measuring Epistemic Resilience of LLMs Under Misleading Medical Context
evidence.outcome: Whether licensing-exam-level scores predict safe medical judgment under misleading context
evidence.effect: Models abandon originally correct answers when misleading context is injected; accuracy drops from 71.1% to 38.0%, showing exam-style benchmark performance overstates robustness.
evidence.quote: We show this assumption is fragile: when misleading context is injected into questions that LLMs originally answer correctly, they abandon the correct answer.

evidence.title: EHRNote-ChatQA: A Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Multi-Turn Clinical Question Answering over Longitudinal Discharge Summaries
evidence.outcome: Whether single-turn clinical QA performance transfers to multi-turn, evidence-grounded discharge-summary QA
evidence.effect: Across 22 LLMs, single-turn clinical QA performance did not reliably transfer to the multi-turn setting; evidence grounding was harder than content answering, and multi-turn errors compounded. No numbers in abstract.
evidence.quote: Benchmarking 22 open- and closed-source LLMs reveals several challenges, including that LLMs struggle more with evidence grounding than content answering, multi-turn errors compound across turns, and single-turn clinical QA performance does not reliably transfer to this setting.

evidence.title: Compositional Reasoning Depth Predicts Clinical AI Failure: Empirical Evidence Consistent with Transformer Compositionality Limits in Electronic Health Record Question Answering
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on clinician-generated EHR questions by reasoning hop count
evidence.effect: Accuracy declined monotonically with hop count across all three models: Claude Sonnet 30.6% to 17.6%, GPT-4o 37.8% to 14.7%, GPT-5.4 37.8% to 23.5%.
evidence.quote: All three models, spanning two providers and two OpenAI generations (GPT-4 and GPT-5), show monotone accuracy decline with hop count: Claude Sonnet zero-shot falls from 30.6% (hop=1) to 17.6% (hop=4) (Cochran-Armitage z=-2.30, p=0.011; OR per hop 0.72, 95% CI [0.56,0.92], p=0.008); GPT-4o replicates this (37.8% to 14.7%; OR 0.58 [0.45,0.75], p<0.001); and gpt-5.4-2026-03-05 confirms it (37.8% to 23.5%; OR 0.80 [0.66,0.98], p=0.027).

evidence.title: CLExEval: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for Qualitative Evaluation of LLM Clinical Reasoning
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy under progressive information masking and reasoning-to-output mismatch versus expert annotations
evidence.effect: GPT-4o-mini accuracy dropped from 95.0% to 32.5% under information scarcity; 68.6% reasoning-to-output mismatch; standalone automated evaluations can substantially overestimate clinical reliability.
evidence.quote: These results suggest that standalone automated clinical evaluations can substantially overestimate clinical reliability without expert-grounded validation.
evidence.sample_unit: rare diagnostic cases (200 reasoning traces; 5,600 expert-physician annotations)

evidence.title: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
evidence.outcome: Rubric pass rates on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks, by criterion weight
evidence.effect: Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.38 (GPT), 0.37 (Gemini); critical weight-5 criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7% versus 80-90% for weight-1 criteria; 55 of 108 critical criteria satisfied by no model.
evidence.quote: The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%.
evidence.sample_unit: clinician-authored clinical scenarios (184 rubric criteria; 552 graded criteria)

evidence.title: Information-seeking failures of large language models in agentic clinical reasoning
evidence.outcome: Overall accuracy of frontier LLMs on agentic hematologic oncology reasoning benchmark
evidence.effect: Across 32 frontier models, the best achieved only 68% overall accuracy despite high scores on medical knowledge assessments.
evidence.quote: Across 32 frontier models, the best achieved only 68% overall accuracy.

evidence.title: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Understand OCT?
evidence.outcome: MLLM performance on OCT understanding benchmark across perception, cognition, reasoning
evidence.effect: Current models remain substantially short of reliable OCT understanding; neither medical-domain adaptation nor increased model scale consistently improves performance across capability levels.
evidence.quote: Experimental results demonstrate that current models remain substantially short of reliable OCT understanding.

evidence.title: Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts
evidence.outcome: Whether general aggregate benchmarks mask clinically consequential failures without domain-specific evaluation
evidence.effect: Absence of domain-specific analyses plus aggregate metrics systematically obscures watermark-induced degradations in clinical text; domain-specific evaluation is called a prerequisite for safe deployment.
evidence.quote: Notably, we find that the absence of domain-specific analyses, combined with aggregate metrics that miss failures inherent to clinical text, can systematically obscure practical watermark-induced degradations.
evidence.sample_unit: not reported (5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on medical tasks)

evidence.title: Evaluating Multi-Turn Multimodal Diagnostic Reasoning on Challenging Real-World Clinical Cases
evidence.outcome: Multi-turn multimodal diagnostic accuracy and reasoning quality of MLLMs on real-world cases
evidence.effect: Proprietary models had highest overall diagnostic accuracy, but the proportion of completely correct diagnoses remained limited across all models; reasoning quality showed considerable limitations.
evidence.quote: Results showed that proprietary models achieved the highest overall diagnostic accuracy, but the proportion of completely correct diagnoses remained limited across all models.

evidence.title: EarlyDx: An Admission-Anchored Benchmark for Open-Ended Generation of Evidence-Supported ED-Encounter Diagnoses
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic recall on admission-time evidence, especially inference-dependent diagnoses
evidence.effect: Zero-shot models recover only 3-31% of diagnoses that must be inferred; post-training raises inference-dependent recall to 56%; no system attains a clinician's balance of sensitivity and precision on time-critical conditions.
evidence.quote: Zero-shot models score largely by extraction, recovering only 3-31% of diagnoses that must be inferred rather than read from the record; post-training raises inference-dependent recall to 56%, but a sizeable margin remains, and on time-critical conditions no system attains a clinician's balance of sensitivity and precision.

evidence.title: Evaluating Counterfactual Sensitivity to Patient Information in Medication-Safety Reasoning
evidence.outcome: Whether static medication-safety accuracy reflects patient-specific reliability
evidence.effect: Models scored well on fixed guideline-following questions (mean 63.6%) but fell to 45.1% on paired counterfactual questions. The authors conclude static accuracy is limited for assessing patient-specific reliability.
evidence.quote: MedPIC-Bench therefore makes conditional rule application measurable and highlights the limitations of static medication-safety accuracy for assessing patient-specific reliability.

evidence.title: CARE-Bench: Benchmarking Patient-Facing LLM Triage
evidence.outcome: LLM triage macro-F1 on a source-grounded benchmark of intended-use action selection
evidence.effect: Unprompted macro-F1 ranged from 31.2 to 50.4; prompted 46.9 to 63.4, with substantial threshold errors remaining.
evidence.quote: Unprompted macro-F1 remains low, ranging from 31.2 to 50.4.

evidence.title: CliniCARE-Bench: Clinical Calibrated Audit of Medical Reasoning in EHR
evidence.outcome: Raw verdict accuracy versus defect-free accuracy (correct verdict without prohibited shortcuts) across agentic systems
evidence.effect: Four-way accuracy spans 65.3-76.1%, but defect-free accuracy is 4.8-14.8 points lower and reorders the leaderboard, so raw accuracy overstates investigation quality.
evidence.quote: Defect-free accuracy, which credits a verdict only when correct and free of prohibited shortcuts, is 4.8-14.8 points lower and reorders the leaderboard.

evidence.title: Will My Assistant Remember My Allergy? What Personal LLM Assistants Forget When Conversation Memory Is Compressed
evidence.outcome: Retention of a passing-mentioned allergy under KV-cache compression, with question hidden versus known
evidence.effect: When the question is hidden until after compression, a passing allergy mention survives 0-1% of the time versus 97% with full memory; prior benchmarks report retention at a 20% budget.
evidence.quote: Hide the question until after compression and the advantage vanishes: on PA-Bench, 100 assistant conversations we construct, an allergy mentioned in passing survives to the question that needs it 0--1% of the time, against 97% with full memory.

evidence.title: Can LLMs Follow Medical Expert Logic? A Benchmark for Hierarchical Logical Consistency in Risk-of-Bias Assessment
evidence.outcome: Benchmark versus end-to-end logical consistency of LLMs in risk-of-bias assessment
evidence.effect: Top model reached 98.88% Atomic Consistency but end-to-end consistency collapsed to 45.13%; several open-weight models fell to nearly 0%.
evidence.quote: Experiments on 10 state-of-the-art LLMs reveal a catastrophic Error Compounding Effect: despite the top model reaching 98.88% Atomic Consistency, its end-to-end consistency collapses to 45.13%, with several open-weight architectures plummeting to nearly 0%.

evidence.title: MedRoundsQA: A Persona and Difficulty Aware Evaluation for Multi-Turn Medical Consultations
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy drop from single-turn benchmark to multi-turn consultation
evidence.effect: Moving from single-turn diagnosis to multi-turn consultations caused degradations of roughly 13-39 points, showing single-turn benchmarks overstate competence.
evidence.quote: (i) moving from a single-turn diagnosis on the standardized records to multi-turn consultations causes large degradations of roughly 13-39 points
evidence.sample_unit: board-exam cases (converted to 24-slot records and simulated dialogues)

evidence.title: Tasks over Application Manuals: Revealing Gaps in Long-Horizon Procedural Reasoning for Language Models
evidence.outcome: Exact-match accuracy on long-horizon ICD-10-CM coding and sentencing tasks versus existing short-horizon benchmarks
evidence.effect: Best exact-match performance with GPT-5 was 1% on ICD-10-CM coding and 15.5% on sentencing tasks, suggesting existing benchmarks overestimate LLM ability.
evidence.quote: These results show that current benchmarks may overestimate LLM reasoning ability and miss a key challenge: reliably following long, rule-based procedures.

evidence.title: LLMs Anchor on Chief Complaint and Fail to Integrate Evidence in Sequential Clinical Triage
evidence.outcome: LLM triage agreement (QWK) on completed records versus sequential checkpoints
evidence.effect: All six LLMs fell from moderate-to-substantial agreement on completed records to fair-to-moderate at every sequential checkpoint. Best model QWK was 0.295 versus 0.887-0.929 for three expert clinicians.
evidence.quote: Deploying LLMs for ED triage based on offline benchmarks alone misses this sequential failure.

evidence.title: Right Answer, Wrong Reason: Accuracy, Consistency, and Consensus Are Misleading Indicators of LLM Faithfulness in Clinical Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Whether exam-style accuracy reflects faithful reasoning in LLMs
evidence.effect: Correct answers had lower CFS than incorrect answers (0.212 vs. 0.398); only 23.3% of cited concepts were causally necessary.
evidence.quote: Correct answers had lower CFS than incorrect answers (0.212 vs. 0.398)
evidence.sample_unit: model-question observations (150 MedQA-USMLE questions x 6 LLMs)

evidence.title: Unmasking True Clinical Competence: The Importance of Adaptive and Open-Ended Evaluation for Large Language Models in Cardiology
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on multiple-choice exam vs open-ended and clinically modified questions
evidence.effect: MC answers 93.0%, reasoning 92.4%; open-ended answers 80.0%, reasoning 80.5% (p<0.001); modified MC answers 93.9% to 66.7%, reasoning 93.9% to 71.2% (both p<0.001).
evidence.quote: Using existing MC question formats substantially overestimates the performance and clinical reasoning capabilities of GPT o1-preview.

evidence.title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Binary Classification of Pediatric Chest X-Rays: A Comparative Evaluation Using a Public Pneumonia Dataset
evidence.outcome: Binary pneumonia classification performance of general-purpose multimodal LLMs on pediatric chest X-rays
evidence.effect: Most models showed high sensitivity but poor specificity (GPT-4o 18%, Gemini 25%, Claude 0%), indicating a strong false-positive tendency.
evidence.quote: Claude 4 Sonnet classified all images as pneumonia (100% sensitivity, 0% specificity).

evidence.title: Performance of a Large Language Model in BI-RADS Classification of Ultrasound Based Breast Lesions
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of general-purpose LLM in BI-RADS classification of breast ultrasound versus radiologist ground truth
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy 19.01%; ROC-AUC 0.5-0.6 across categories; malignancy-probable categories (4b-5) akin to random chance; predictions typically 1-2 categories off.
evidence.quote: We found that the overall accuracy of Gemini 2.0 was 19.01% in predicting the BI-RADS classification of the breast lesions, and those of each category did not significantly differ from one another.

evidence.title: Probing the Surgical Competence of LLMs: A global health study leveraging AfriMedQA benchmarks
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on specialty-specific benchmark questions, including surgery, pathology, and obstetrics
evidence.effect: Top models (o1, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) exceeded 82% mean accuracy but consistently underperformed in surgery, pathology, and obstetrics compared with medical disciplines.
evidence.quote: Top models (o1, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) achieved mean accuracies exceeding 82%, showing strong diagnostic reasoning, yet consistently underperformed in surgery, pathology, and obstetrics compared with medical disciplines.
evidence.country: Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and other African countries (AfriMed-QA benchmark; authored by African medical professors)

evidence.title: Not One Size Fits All: The Selective Effect of Reasoning Processes for Multimodal Body Language Emotion Recognition in GAI
evidence.outcome: Emotion recognition performance of Gemini models versus human benchmark on body-language stimuli
evidence.effect: Gemini Pro 2.0 CCR = 0.722, on par with human benchmark (0.717); FlashThinking CCR = 0.463, failing to outperform generalist models.
evidence.quote: Instead, the high-capacity generalist model (Gemini Pro 2.0) exhibited the highest performance (CCR = 0.722, 95% CI [0.590, 0.838]), significantly outperforming all other models (OR ≤ 0.19, p < .001) and achieving parity with human benchmarks (CCR = 0.717).
evidence.sample_unit: stimuli (EU-Emotion Stimulus Set body language items)

evidence.title: Auditing frontier general-purpose large language models in biomedical tasks: reasoning gains, extraction limits, and benchmark reliability
evidence.outcome: Whether benchmark results reflect deployment-relevant reliability
evidence.effect: Benchmarks may misestimate model capability and misguide deployment decisions. Format-constrained extraction and evidence-dense summarization remain limited despite reasoning gains.
evidence.quote: suggesting that current benchmarks may misestimate model capability and potentially misguide deployment decisions

evidence.title: Beyond Benchmarks: Dynamic, Automatic And Systematic Red-Teaming Agents For Trustworthy Medical Language Models
evidence.outcome: Gap between static benchmark scores and dynamic reliability, including ranking shifts across evaluations
evidence.effect: Profound gap between high static benchmark performance and low dynamic reliability (the 'Benchmarking Gap'). Top models had failure rates over 70% on HealthBench, with stark ranking shifts.
evidence.quote: Applying DAS to 15 proprietary and open-source LLMs revealed a profound gap between high static benchmark performance and low dynamic reliability - the ''Benchmarking Gap''.

evidence.title: Frontier Large Language Models for Comprehensive Medication Review in CKD Patients with Polypharmacy: A Trap-Embedded Synthetic Benchmark
evidence.outcome: Open-ended CKD medication review performance versus multiple-choice benchmark expectations
evidence.effect: Macro F1 ranged 0.41 to 0.49; open-ended scoring exposed LLM failures invisible to multiple-choice benchmarks, so generic benchmarks overstate competence.
evidence.quote: This nephrology-specific benchmark exposes clinically important LLM blind spots that generic multiple-choice evaluations would not detect.

evidence.title: MedMisBench: Measuring Epistemic Resilience of LLMs Under Misleading Medical Context
evidence.outcome: Gap between licensing-exam-level scores and safe judgment under misleading context
evidence.effect: LLMs reaching expert-level exam scores abandon correct answers under misleading context; accuracy fell from 71.1% to 38.0%.
evidence.quote: We show this assumption is fragile: when misleading context is injected into questions that LLMs originally answer correctly, they abandon the correct answer.

evidence.title: Accuracy of GPT-3.5, GPT-4.0, and GPT-5.0 in Neurosurgery-Related Questions: A Comparative Study Including Self-Correction Analysis
evidence.outcome: Benchmark exam-style accuracy of GPT models on neurosurgery multiple-choice questions
evidence.effect: GPT-5.0 78.0% combined accuracy vs GPT-3.5 61.8% and GPT-4.0 60.8%; overall accuracy remains below 80%, and authors note limited clinical applicability.
evidence.quote: However, overall accuracy remains below 80%, and the absence of human benchmarking and the single-trial design limit direct clinical applicability.
evidence.sample_unit: question evaluations (250 questions x 2 languages x 3 models)

evidence.title: Retrieval-Augmented Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5 Surpass Human Performance on the Nuclear Cardiology Board Preparation Exam (and Claude Drafts a Paper About it)
evidence.outcome: Refusals by safety filters on exam questions in deployed configuration
evidence.effect: GPT-5.5 refused a mean of 12.2 questions (7.3%) per iteration due to safety filters.
evidence.quote: GPT-5.5 achieved 86.7% ± 2.2% (text 88.5%, image 77.0%) but refused a mean of 12.2 questions (7.3%) per iteration due to safety filters.

evidence.title: Benchmarking Language Models for Clinical Safety: A Primer for Mental Health Professionals
evidence.outcome: Whether a single benchmark score reflects clinical competence given configuration and measurement floor
evidence.effect: Total scores ranged from 19.5 to 84.0 (expert baseline 32.5); best model approached the instrument's measurement floor; a single score can support markedly different claims depending on configuration.
evidence.quote: A single benchmark score can support markedly different claims depending on the assumed standard of clinical behavior, the instrument’s remaining measurement range, and the configuration that produced the result.

evidence.title: On the robustness of medical term representations in locally deployable language models
evidence.outcome: Robust representation of neurological terms across model size, fine-tuning and complexity
evidence.effect: Robustness followed log-linear scaling with size (r=0.736); fine-tuning gave no benefit at 4B but raised 27B from 38.2% to 62.6%; most models degraded sharply with rising term complexity.
evidence.quote: While representational robustness broadly follows model size scaling laws, neither model size nor fine-tuning guarantees clinical reliability.

evidence.title: High Consistency, Limited Accuracy: Evaluating Large Language Models for Binary Medical Diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of general-purpose LLMs on heart disease cases despite high exam scores
evidence.effect: Diagnostic accuracy about 50%, equivalent to random guessing, despite 60-80% on licensing exams; consistency-accuracy gap of about 50 percentage points.
evidence.quote: However, diagnostic accuracy remained at approximately 50%, equivalent to random guessing.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical cases (UCI Heart Disease dataset; 1,200 total predictions)

evidence.title: Comparative Performance of General-Purpose Large Language Models and a Specialized Clinical AI Tool on OKAP-Style Ophthalmology Questions
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of LLMs on ophthalmology exam-style questions versus real clinical competence
evidence.effect: Gemini-Pro-3 95.8% accuracy; all other models significantly lower adjusted odds of correct response; accuracy declined with difficulty. Authors note real-world clinical scenarios still needed.
evidence.quote: These findings suggest that a clinical specialization LLM does not guarantee superior performance in ophthalmic knowledge, and further studies using real-world clinical scenarios are needed to evaluate LLM-based systems in ophthalmology.

evidence.title: Retrieval‑Augmented Clinical Question‑Answering System for Bariatric Surgery Built on the ASMBS Textbook: From Good to Great
evidence.outcome: Raw LLM accuracy on domain benchmark showing residual errors in unaided models
evidence.effect: Raw accuracy was 70.5% (GPT-4o-mini), 81.0% (GPT-4), and 87.0% (GPT-5) on the 200-question benchmark.
evidence.quote: GPT-4 with RAG reached 89.5% versus 81.0% raw (+ 8.5 pp; +13 questions), and GPT-4o-mini improved from 70.5% to 84.5% with RAG (+ 14.0 pp; +28 questions).

evidence.title: Vision and Language Models for Classifying Maxillary Sinus Disease on Cone-Beam Computed Tomography: A Transparent Multimodal Benchmark
evidence.outcome: Apparent benchmark performance of raw AI text versus verified performance
evidence.effect: Raw ChatGPT text gave language-model AUC 0·992 to 1·000, but performance fell substantially against radiologist-confirmed labels (BERT-base AUC 0·999 to 0·837), overstating true competence.
evidence.quote: On the 297-case pre/post analysis, this advantage depended heavily on label source: language and text-derived VLM performance fell substantially from ChatGPT-only to radiologist-confirmed labels (e.g. BERT-base AUC 0·999 to 0·837), while vision-model performance was stable or modestly improved (e.g. DenseNet-121 0·867 to 0·891).

evidence.title: Evaluating GPT-4o Model Proficiency and Clinical Reasoning for Antimicrobial Stewardship in Dentistry
evidence.outcome: Benchmark-style question accuracy versus real-world suitability for clinical use
evidence.effect: GPT-4o scored 72% on multiple-choice questions, but residual risks mean it is not suitable for unsupervised clinical use.
evidence.quote: However, residual risks indicate that it is not suitable for unsupervised clinical use but shows potential as a supervised AMS educational tool.

evidence.title: Evaluating Capabilities of Large Language Models: Performance of GPT4 on Surgical Knowledge Assessments
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT-4 on surgical knowledge exam questions
evidence.effect: ChatGPT correctly answered 71% and 68% of multiple-choice SCORE and Data-B questions; errors included inaccurate information in complex (36.4%) and fact-based (25.0%) questions.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT correctly answered 71% and 68% of multiple-choice SCORE and Data-B questions, respectively.

evidence.title: Performance of Multimodal GPT-4V on USMLE with Image: Potential for Imaging Diagnostic Support with Explanations
evidence.outcome: GPT-4V accuracy on exam questions with images across USMLE, DRQCE, AMBOSS and subdomains
evidence.effect: Accuracy 86.2% USMLE, 73.1% DRQCE, 62.0% AMBOSS; subdomain accuracy varied from 100% (immunology, otolaryngology) to 25% (anatomy, emergency medicine).
evidence.quote: On the other hand, GPT-4V's performance varied across different medical subdomains, with the highest accuracy in immunology (100%) and otolaryngology (100%) and the lowest accuracy in anatomy (25%) and emergency medicine (25%).

evidence.title: Unveiling the Clinical Incapabilities: A Benchmarking Study of GPT-4V(ision) for Ophthalmic Multimodal Image Analysis
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, usability and safety of GPT-4V responses on ophthalmic clinical tasks
evidence.effect: Of 600 responses, 30.6% accurate, 21.5% highly usable, 55.6% no harm; diagnosis accuracy 16.1%, decision support 24.0%.
evidence.quote: Out of 600 responses, 30.6% were accurate, 21.5% were highly usable, and 55.6% were deemed as no harm.

evidence.title: ChatGPT for automating lung cancer staging: feasibility study on open radiology report dataset
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT TNM staging from radiology reports against radiologist consensus
evidence.effect: Best accuracy was GPT-4 with TNM rule in the prompt: 52.2% (T), 78.9% (N), 86.7% (M); errors from numerical reasoning and anatomical or lexical knowledge gaps.
evidence.quote: The best accuracy scores were achieved by GPT-4 when it was presented with the TNM classification rule (52.2%, 78.9%, and 86.7% for the T, N, and M categories).
evidence.sample_unit: CT radiology reports (subset used for evaluation after prompt tuning)

evidence.title: Assessing GPT-4’s Diagnostic Accuracy with Darker Skin Tones: Underperformance and Implications
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 dermatology diagnostic accuracy compared with previously reported accuracies
evidence.effect: Overall GPT-4 correctly diagnosed 28% (14/50) of images; correct diagnosis in top differentials for 48% (24/50), much lower than prior reports up to 90%.
evidence.quote: Overall, GPT-4 correctly diagnosed the condition in 28% of the images (n=14/50), while the correct diagnosis was included in its list of top differentials for 48% of the images (n=24/50).

evidence.title: Do Language Models Think Like Doctors?
evidence.outcome: LLM performance on script concordance test clinical reasoning versus typical medical multiple-choice benchmark performance
evidence.effect: LLMs scored markedly lower on SCTs than on MCQ benchmarks; GPT-4o 63.6%, Claude-3.5 Sonnet 58.8%, o1-preview 58.5%, Gemini-1.5-Pro 54.4%; below senior residents and attendings.
evidence.quote: LLMs demonstrated markedly lower performance on SCTs compared to their typical achievement on medical multiple choice benchmarks.

evidence.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Pass the American Board of Orthopaedic Surgery Examination? Orthopaedic Residents Versus ChatGPT
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT accuracy on orthopaedic in-training exam questions versus resident percentiles and pass threshold
evidence.effect: ChatGPT answered 47% (97 of 207) correctly; scored 40th percentile for PGY1s, 8th for PGY2s, 1st for PGY3-5; unlikely to pass written boards. Accuracy fell with taxonomy level (54%, 51%, 34%; p = 0.034).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT selected the correct answer 47% (97 of 207) of the time, and 53% (110 of 207) of the time it answered incorrectly.

evidence.title: Performance of Generative Large Language Models on Ophthalmology Board-Style Questions
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on ophthalmology board-style questions versus human respondents, and hallucination frequency
evidence.effect: Human accuracy 72.2%; ChatGPT-3.5 58.8%, ChatGPT-4.0 71.6%, Bing Chat 71.2%. Hallucination/nonlogical reasoning: 42.4%, 18.0%, 25.6% respectively.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-3.5 had the highest rate of hallucinations and nonlogical reasoning (42.4%), followed by ChatGPT-4.0 (18.0%) and Bing Chat (25.6%).

evidence.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
evidence.outcome: Gap between multiple-choice benchmark accuracy and human-rated answer quality
evidence.effect: Flan-PaLM reached 67.6% on MedQA, surpassing the prior state of the art by more than 17%, yet human evaluation revealed key gaps. Med-PaLM remained inferior to clinicians.
evidence.quote: However, human evaluation reveals key gaps.

evidence.title: Performance and exploration of ChatGPT in medical examination, records and education in Chinese: Pave the way for medical AI
evidence.outcome: Exam-question accuracy of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on Chinese and English licensing exams
evidence.effect: GPT-3.5 accuracy on CNMLE, ENMLE, NEEPM was 56%, 76%, 62%; GPT-4 was 84%, 86%, 82%. Exam scores only, not deployed clinical competencies.
evidence.quote: The accuracy of GPT-3.5 in CNMLE, ENMLE, and NEEPM was 56% (56/100), 76% (76/100), and 62% (62/100), respectively, compared to that of GPT-4, which was of 84% (84/100), 86% (86/100), and 82% (82/100).
evidence.sample_unit: exam questions per dataset (CNMLE, ENMLE, NEEPM); plus 10 discharge summaries and 10 group-learning sessions

evidence.title: Unveiling the ChatGPT phenomenon: Evaluating the consistency and accuracy of endodontic question answers
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT answers to endodontic questions versus expert answers
evidence.effect: Average accuracy 57.33%; significant differences by difficulty, with lower accuracy for easier questions.
evidence.quote: In terms of answer accuracy, ChatGPT achieved an average accuracy of 57.33%.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Current Ability of ChatGPT to Assist in Professional Otolaryngology Education
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT-3.5 accuracy on otolaryngology board-level questions rated by expert otolaryngologists
evidence.effect: Open-ended: 56.7% completely accurate initially, 73.3% on repeat; multiple-choice only 43.3% correct.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT currently does not provide reliably accurate responses to sophisticated questions in Otolaryngology.

evidence.title: Stratified Evaluation of GPT's Question Answering in Surgery Reveals Artificial Intelligence (AI) Knowledge Gaps
evidence.outcome: GPT accuracy on surgical MCQs versus full MedMCQA benchmark
evidence.effect: GPT-3.5 53.3% and GPT-4 64.4% on surgical questions; GPT-4 performed worse on surgical questions than on the whole dataset, GPT-3.5 the opposite.
evidence.quote: When compared to their performance on the full MedMCQA dataset, the two models performed differently: GPT-4 performed worse on surgical questions than on the dataset as a whole, while GPT-3.5 showed the opposite pattern.

evidence.title: The ability of artificial intelligence tools to formulate orthopaedic clinical decisions in comparison to human clinicians: An analysis of ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4, and Bard
evidence.outcome: Alignment of LLM orthopaedic treatment choices with most popular surgeon responses on real cases
evidence.effect: Most-popular-response agreement: ChatGPT 4 68.0%, ChatGPT 3.5 40.2%, Bard 45.4% (P<0.001); poorer on controversial questions.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT 4 demonstrated the highest proportion of most popular responses (proportion of most popular response: ChatGPT 4 68.0%, ChatGPT 3.5 40.2%, Bard 45.4%, P value < 0.001), outperforming other AI tools.

evidence.title: A Novel Evaluation Model for Assessing ChatGPT on Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Certification Examinations: Performance Study
evidence.outcome: Exam-based competency of ChatGPT on open-ended OHNS board questions
evidence.effect: ChatGPT achieved a passing mark (average 75% across 3 trials); concordance 92.06%; hallucinations and self-conflicting answers observed.
evidence.quote: In an open-ended question assessment, ChatGPT achieved a passing mark (an average of 75% across 3 trials) in the attempts and demonstrated higher accuracy with prompts.

evidence.title: Danger, Danger, Gaston Labat! Does zero-shot artificial intelligence correlate with anticoagulation guidelines recommendations for neuraxial anesthesia?
evidence.outcome: GPT-3.5 accuracy on guideline-based neuraxial bleeding risk assessment versus truth table
evidence.effect: Baseline performance slightly above chance; with detailed prompts and explicit guidelines, AUC 0.70 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.77); performance varied among medication classes.
evidence.quote: Baseline performance of GPT-3.5 was slightly above chance.

evidence.title: Performance of Progressive Generations of GPT on an Exam Designed for Certifying Physicians as Certified Clinical Densitometrists
evidence.venue: Journal of clinical densitometry : the official journal of the International Society for Clinical Densitometry
evidence.outcome: Exam score of general LLMs on specialist certification practice exam
evidence.effect: GPT-3 answered 62 questions correctly (failing score 289); GPT-4 answered 82 correctly (passing score 342); GPT-4 scored 65% on Imaging Technology in Bone Health.
evidence.quote: GPT-3 answered 62 questions correctly resulting in a failing ISCD score of 289. However, GPT-4 answered 82 questions correctly with a passing score of 342.

evidence.title: Step into the era of large multimodal models: a pilot study on ChatGPT-4V(ision)'s ability to interpret radiological images
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-4V on USMLE-style image questions, and with history removed
evidence.effect: Accuracy 77.01% on USMLE-style questions; dropped to 19.54% when detailed patient history removed (P<0.0001); AUC 0.768 for chest radiograph abnormality detection.
evidence.quote: Removing detailed patient history dropped the diagnostic accuracy to 19.54% (P<0.0001).

evidence.title: Performance of GPT-4V in Answering the Japanese Otolaryngology Board Certification Examination Questions: Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: GPT-4V accuracy on board certification exam questions across prompt and input types
evidence.effect: Accuracy for text-only input averaged 24.7%, improving to 47.3% with English translation and prompts (P<.001); nonresponse rate 46.3% fell to 2.7%.
evidence.quote: The accuracy rate for text-only input was, on average, 24.7% but improved to 47.3% with the addition of English translation and prompts (P<.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating and Enhancing Large Language Models' Performance in Domain-Specific Medicine: Development and Usability Study With DocOA
evidence.outcome: General LLM performance on domain-specific clinical competencies versus general medical benchmark expectations
evidence.effect: General LLMs had unsatisfactory performance on OA management, with marked decline as tasks shifted from knowledge to personalized treatment recommendations.
evidence.quote: By contrast, general-purpose models such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 exhibit unsatisfactory performance when benchmarked against OA management.
evidence.sample_unit: benchmark questions (337 guideline-item, 145 management-option, 216 treatment-strategy, 80 real-case QA)

evidence.title: Performance of Large Language Models on Medical Oncology Examination Questions
evidence.outcome: Exam-question accuracy versus clinical safety of LLM answers
evidence.effect: Best LLM scored 85.0% on exam questions, yet 18 of 22 incorrect answers (81.8%) had medium or high likelihood of moderate to severe harm if acted upon.
evidence.quote: If acted upon in clinical practice, 18 of 22 incorrect answers (81.8%; 95% CI, 59.7%-94.8%) would have a medium or high likelihood of moderate to severe harm.

evidence.title: Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy and guideline adherence in simulated clinical setting versus licensing-exam performance
evidence.effect: LLMs did not accurately diagnose across all pathologies, performed significantly worse than physicians, followed neither diagnostic nor treatment guidelines, and could not interpret laboratory results.
evidence.quote: We show that current state-of-the-art LLMs do not accurately diagnose patients across all pathologies (performing significantly worse than physicians), follow neither diagnostic nor treatment guidelines, and cannot interpret laboratory results, thus posing a serious risk to the health of patients.

evidence.title: Claude 3 Opus and ChatGPT With GPT-4 in Dermoscopic Image Analysis for Melanoma Diagnosis: Comparative Performance Analysis
evidence.outcome: Melanoma diagnostic accuracy of general-purpose LLMs on dermoscopic images from a public archive
evidence.effect: Primary diagnosis accuracy was 56% for Claude 3 Opus and 48% for ChatGPT; malignancy discrimination sensitivity was 47.06% and 45.1%, respectively.
evidence.quote: Both models made errors in diagnosing melanoma and benign lesions.
