evidence.title: Comparative Evaluation of LLMs in Clinical Oncology
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on oncology questions versus human exam benchmark
evidence.effect: Only GPT-4 performed above the 50th percentile of the human benchmark; performance was worse in clinical oncology subcategories than in foundational topics; all LLMs had clinically significant error rates.
evidence.quote: Relative to a human benchmark (2013 and 2014 examination results), GPT-4 was the only model to perform above the 50th percentile.

evidence.title: Interpretation of Clinical Retinal Images Using an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
evidence.outcome: Proportion of retina cases correctly diagnosed by custom GPT-4 chatbot using multimodal images
evidence.effect: Correct diagnosis in 35 of 69 cases (50.7%); needed full patient description for 23 of 35 correct cases (65.7%); OR 10.1 (95% CI 3.3-30.3) for full description vs age and sex only.
evidence.quote: The diagnostic ability of the chatbot in interpretation of multimodal imaging without text-based information is currently limited.

evidence.title: Currently Available Large Language Models Do Not Provide Musculoskeletal Treatment Recommendations That Are Concordant With Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines
evidence.venue: Arthroscopy : the journal of arthroscopic & related surgery : official publication of the Arthroscopy Association of North America and the International Arthroscopy Association
evidence.outcome: Off-the-shelf LLM clinical competence on guideline-based treatment recommendations
evidence.effect: More than 1-in-4 recommendations (29.7% indeterminate or discordant) did not reflect CPGs; concordance ranged 58.3% to 79.2% across four LLMs.
evidence.quote: Among leading commercially available LLMs, more than 1-in-4 recommendations concerning the evaluation and management of rotator cuff and anterior cruciate ligament injuries do not reflect current evidence-based CPGs.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (48 AAOS guideline recommendations x 4 LLMs)

evidence.title: The Potential of Chat-Based Artificial Intelligence Models in Differentiating Between Keloid and Hypertrophic Scars: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of chatbots on scar images (keloid vs hypertrophic scar)
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy of GPT-4 and Bing Chat was 36.0% and 22.0% respectively (P = 0.027); authors conclude technology is not yet sufficient for clinical application standards.
evidence.quote: The overall accuracy rates of GPT-4 and Bing Chat were 36.0% and 22.0%, respectively (P = 0.027), with GPT-4 showing better performance in terms of specificity for keloids (0.6 vs. 0.006) and hypertrophic scars (0.72 vs. 0.0) than Bing Chat.
evidence.sample_unit: mock scar images (each queried five times per chatbot)

evidence.title: The future of AI clinicians: assessing the modern standard of chatbots and their approach to diagnostic uncertainty
evidence.outcome: Chatbot accuracy on diagnostic uncertainty questions versus Family Medicine residents
evidence.effect: Both chatbots scored lower than residents (p < 0.01). Claude-3 57.7% (52/90) and GPT-4o 53.3% (48/90) versus PGY-1 61.1% and PGY-2 63.3%.
evidence.quote: Compared to the residents, both chatbots scored lower on diagnostic uncertainty questions (p < 0.01).

evidence.title: Assessing the accuracy and consistency of answers by ChatGPT to questions regarding carbon monoxide poisoning
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT accuracy on single-choice carbon monoxide poisoning exam questions in Chinese and English
evidence.effect: Accuracy was 61.1% in Chinese and 57% in English against the question bank reference answers.
evidence.quote: Meanwhile, the accuracy of these responses was less favorable, with an accuracy rate of 61.1% in Chinese and 57% in English.
evidence.sample_unit: single-choice questions (each entered 10 times in Chinese and English)

evidence.title: Comparative Analysis of Generative Pre-Trained Transformer Models in Oncogene-Driven Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Introducing the Generative Artificial Intelligence Performance Score
evidence.outcome: Generative model performance on intended-use oncology treatment recommendations against NCCN guidelines
evidence.effect: GPT-4 hallucinated in 34% of responses and GPT-3.5 in 53%; GPT-4 G-PS 0.34, GPT-3.5 -0.15.
evidence.quote: Although the rate of hallucinations improved in the GPT-4 model, future generative AI use in clinical care requires high levels of accuracy with minimal to no room for hallucinations.

evidence.title: Medical large language models are vulnerable to data-poisoning attacks
evidence.outcome: Whether public medical benchmark scores reveal poisoned-model harms
evidence.effect: Corrupted models matched corruption-free counterparts on open-source medical benchmarks routinely used to evaluate medical LLMs, despite producing more medical errors.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, we discover that corrupted models match the performance of their corruption-free counterparts on open-source benchmarks routinely used to evaluate medical LLMs.
evidence.sample_unit: LLMs trained (1.3B and 4B parameter) with simulated poisoning of The Pile

evidence.title: Evaluation of LLMs accuracy and consistency in the registered dietitian exam through prompt engineering and knowledge retrieval
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on registered dietitian exam questions by prompt type and proficiency level
evidence.effect: LLMs obtained acceptable overall performance but results varied considerably with different prompts and question domains; RAP was particularly effective for GPT-4o on Expert level questions.
evidence.quote: Our findings revealed that while these LLMs obtained acceptable overall performance, their results varied considerably with different prompts and question domains.

evidence.title: Unveiling GPT-4V's hidden challenges behind high accuracy on USMLE questions: Observational Study
evidence.outcome: Gap between exam-question accuracy and explanation quality/image interpretation of GPT-4V
evidence.effect: High accuracy (73.1-88.9%) but among incorrect answers 18.2% (10/55) inaccurate text, 45.5% (25/55) inference errors, 76.3% (42/55) image misunderstandings.
evidence.quote: However, incorrect answers often had poor explanation quality: 18.2% (10/55) contained inaccurate text, 45.5% (25/55) had inference errors, and 76.3% (42/55) demonstrated image misunderstandings.

evidence.title: A preliminary investigation into the potential, pitfalls, and limitations of large language models for mammography interpretation
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 mammography interpretation accuracy on intended-use clinical task
evidence.effect: Projection identified correctly in 53.3% of cases; sensitivity 50.0%, specificity 37.5%; significant false positives, false negatives, and hallucinations.
evidence.quote: The study highlighted GPT-4's embryonic interpretative abilities with a sensitivity of 50.0% and specificity of 37.5%.

evidence.title: Competency of Large Language Models in Evaluating Appropriate Responses to Suicidal Ideation: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: LLM competency in rating appropriateness of responses to suicidal ideation versus expert suicidologists (SIRI-2)
evidence.effect: All 3 LLMs rated responses more appropriate than experts (mean diff 0.86 ChatGPT, 0.61 Claude, 0.73 Gemini); outliers 19%, 11%, 36%; Claude and ChatGPT matched or exceeded professionals.
evidence.quote: Current versions of 3 major LLMs demonstrated an upward bias in their evaluations of appropriate responses to suicidal ideation; however, 2 of the 3 models performed equivalent to or exceeded the performance of mental health professionals.
evidence.sample_unit: clinician responses to suicidal ideation scenarios rated by each LLM (SIRI-2 items)

evidence.title: ChatGPT-4's Accuracy in Estimating Thyroid Nodule Features and Cancer Risk From Ultrasound Images
evidence.venue: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists
evidence.outcome: GPT-4/GPT-4o accuracy identifying TI-RADS features and categories on thyroid ultrasound versus radiologist reference standard
evidence.effect: GPT-4 showed high specificity but low sensitivity; benign nodules 25.0% sensitivity, 99.5% specificity; moderately suspicious 75% sensitivity, 22.2% specificity, 42.1% accuracy; isoechoic 5% vs 46%; cropped images performed worse.
evidence.quote: While GPT-4 and GPT-4o models show potential for improving the efficiency of thyroid nodule triage, their performance remains suboptimal, particularly in higher-risk categories.

evidence.title: Can off-the-shelf visual large language models detect and diagnose ocular diseases from retinal photographs?
evidence.outcome: Ophthalmologist-rated quality of VLLM diagnostic descriptions of retinal images
evidence.effect: Only 21.2% of GPT-4V default, 4.8% of GPT-4V data analyst and 28.6% of Gemini responses rated good; all VLLMs inadequate for accurate diagnosis despite 97.1% detection by GPT-4V default.
evidence.quote: Despite the relatively high detection rates, the quality of diagnostic descriptions was generally suboptimal-with only 21.2% of GPT-4V's (default) responses, 4.8% of GPT-4V's (data analyst) responses and 28.6% for Google Gemini's responses rated as good.

evidence.title: Large language models for dermatological image interpretation - a comparative study
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of multimodal LLMs on dermatological images
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy highest for GPT-4o (67.8%), GPT-4o mini 63.8%, Llama3.2 11B 61.4%; erysipelas lowest (33.4% mean); 11.0% of images misdiagnosed by all LLMs.
evidence.quote: The highest overall accuracy was achieved by GPT-4o (67.8 %), followed by GPT-4o mini (63.8 %) and Llama3.2 11B (61.4 %).

evidence.title: Performance of large language models on family medicine licensing exams
evidence.outcome: LLM performance on licensing exam questions, as proxy for clinical competence
evidence.effect: Five models exceeded the 65% passing threshold with simple prompts; seven did so with few-shot prompts; o1-preview reached 85.5%. Authors note multiple-choice formats cannot address broader clinical competencies.
evidence.quote: Five models exceeded the 65% passing threshold under simple prompts; seven did so with few-shot prompts.

evidence.title: Leveraging large language models for patient-ventilator asynchrony detection
evidence.outcome: Direct LLM classification accuracy on flow starvation asynchrony categories from ventilator waveforms
evidence.effect: LLMs performed poorly in direct FS classification (accuracy: GPT-4 0.497; Claude-3.5 0.627; Gemini-1.5 0.544; DeepSeek-R1 0.520).
evidence.quote: LLMs performed poorly in direct FS classification (accuracy: GPT-4: 0.497; Claude-3.5: 0.627; Gemini-1.5: 0.544, DeepSeek-R1: 0.520).

evidence.title: Assessment of ChatGPT-3.5 performance on the medical genetics specialist exam
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT-3.5 accuracy on specialist medical genetics exam questions, by category and complexity
evidence.effect: 59% of 456 questions correct overall; 37% on clinical case-based questions; 63% on simple vs 43% on complex questions (P = .001).
evidence.quote: Accuracy differed by category: 71% for calculation-based questions, approximately 60% for genetic methods and genetic alterations, and only 37% for clinical case-based questions.

evidence.title: Evaluating GPT-4's visual interpretation and clinical reasoning on emergency settings: A 5-year analysis
evidence.venue: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association : JCMA
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 accuracy on emergency medicine board exam questions, including stepwise image-to-decision performance
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy 60.1%; text 60.2%, image 59.3%. Image type identification 100%, findings 86.4%, diagnostic reasoning 83.1%, final decision-making 59.3%.
evidence.quote: However, accuracy declined in diagnostic reasoning (83.1%) and further dropped in final decision-making (59.3%).

evidence.title: [Preliminary exploration of the applications of five large language models in the field of oral auxiliary diagnosis, treatment and health consultation]
evidence.venue: Zhonghua kou qiang yi xue za zhi = Zhonghua kouqiang yixue zazhi = Chinese journal of stomatology
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on dental licensing exam and expert-rated oral health answers
evidence.effect: Average exam accuracy 61.7% (370.2/600); HuatuoGPT 50.8% below passing; 3C scores did not reach full marks (ChatGPT median 3 of 4).
evidence.quote: Howere, their outputs carry a risk of errors (since the 3C scoring results do not reach the full marks), so prudent judgment should be exercised when using them.
evidence.sample_unit: questions (47 diagnosis/treatment + 35 consultation) plus 600 licensing exam questions

evidence.title: Evaluating the Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models for Medical Coding and Hospital Readmission Risk Stratification: Zero-Shot Prompting Approach
evidence.outcome: Zero-shot LLM accuracy on diagnosis, ICD-9 coding, and readmission risk using discharge summaries
evidence.effect: ICD-9 correctness 14.6%-45.3%; readmission risk 33%-72.6%; diagnosis 79%-90%. None of the models met clinical standards across all tasks.
evidence.quote: None of the models met clinical standards across all tasks, and performance in medical coding remained the weakest area across all models.

evidence.title: Performance of Large Language Models in Recognizing Brain MRI Sequences: A Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT-4o, Claude 4 Opus, and Gemini 2.5 Pro
evidence.outcome: MRI sequence classification accuracy of multimodal LLMs on zero-shot benchmark
evidence.effect: Sequence accuracy 97.7% ChatGPT-4o, 93.1% Gemini 2.5 Pro, 73.1% Claude 4 Opus (p<0.001); models vary significantly on specific sequence classification.
evidence.quote: MRI sequence classification accuracy was 97.7% for ChatGPT-4o, 93.1% for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 73.1% for Claude 4 Opus (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: A Comparative Study of Five Large Language Models' Response for Liver Cancer Comprehensive Treatment
evidence.outcome: Clinical applicability of LLM responses to liver cancer questions, professional vs common-sense
evidence.effect: Kimi and GPT-4 had the highest fully applicable responses (68% and 62%); none consistently guideline-concordant; professional-level questions scored significantly lower than common-sense ones.
evidence.quote: However, none of the LLMs consistently provided guideline-concordant answers to all questions.

evidence.title: Comparative Accuracy Assessment of Large Language Models in Cardiothoracic Anesthesia: A Performance Analysis of Claude and ChatGPT-4 on Subspecialty Board-Style Questions
evidence.outcome: Subspecialty benchmark accuracy of general LLMs versus their strong performance on general medical exams
evidence.effect: Both models scored well below the 80% clinical threshold on subspecialty questions (Claude 32%, ChatGPT-4 23%), despite prior proficiency on general medical licensing examinations.
evidence.quote: Both models performed below the threshold typically considered acceptable for clinical decision-making (≥80%).

evidence.title: From algorithms to operating room: can large language models master China's attending anesthesiology exam? A cross-sectional evaluation
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on anesthesiology attending exam questions, with clinical scenario and reasoning subgroups
evidence.effect: DeepSeek-R1 70.6-73.4%, GPT-4 68.6-70.3%, DeepSeek-V3 53.1-55.5%, GPT-3.5 52.2-55.7%; all models struggled with clinical scenarios and advanced reasoning.
evidence.quote: All models excelled in basic knowledge and Type A1 questions but struggled with clinical scenarios and advanced reasoning.

evidence.title: Assessing the Diagnostic Capabilities of ChatGPT-4 Omni in Grading Diabetic Retinopathy Fundoscopy Using Color Fundus Photographs
evidence.outcome: GPT-4o diagnostic accuracy grading diabetic retinopathy from fundus photographs versus FDA-approved AI
evidence.effect: GPT-4o sensitivity 47.7% and specificity 73.8%, significantly lower than FDA-approved AI systems; strong bias toward classifying images as no DR; mild DR accuracy 49.8% in binary tasks.
evidence.quote: When compared to FDA-approved AI systems, GPT-4o's sensitivity (47.7%) and specificity (73.8%) were significantly lower.

evidence.title: Limitations of broadly trained LLMs in interpreting orthopedic Walch glenoid classifications
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of general-purpose LLMs classifying Walch glenoid diagrams
evidence.effect: DeepSeek achieved 44% accuracy (7/16), while Claude had 0% accuracy (0/16); both insufficient for clinical use despite general LLM capability claims.
evidence.quote: DeepSeek achieved 44% accuracy (7/16), while Claude had 0% accuracy (0/16).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (conversation threads) classifying glenoid diagrams

evidence.title: Comparative Diagnostic Performance of a Multimodal Large Language Model Versus a Dedicated Electrocardiogram AI in Detecting Myocardial Infarction From Electrocardiogram Images: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Clinical competence of general-purpose multimodal LLMs on ECG MI detection despite general medical promise
evidence.effect: ChatGPT sensitivity 36.40%, specificity 76.2%; Gemini sensitivity 97.07% but specificity 6.24%; both underperformed dedicated tool.
evidence.quote: LLMs, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, underperform relative to specialized tools such as ECG Buddy in ECG image-based MI diagnosis.
evidence.country: Pakistan (public dataset); study conducted elsewhere not stated

evidence.title: Evaluation of the clinical reasoning of GPT-4o, a multimodal generative artificial intelligence model, in 18 public gastroenterology case studies
evidence.outcome: Exam-style benchmark accuracy versus clinical reasoning quality
evidence.effect: 79.6% accuracy on board exam questions, yet reasoning errors showed omission of information already provided (clinical context, temporal criteria).
evidence.quote: the observed failures revealed that the model tends to omit information already provided (such as clinical context or temporal criteria), thereby compromising the quality of its reasoning.
evidence.sample_unit: multiple-choice questions from 18 board exam clinical cases

evidence.title: Large Language Models Perform at Chance Level in the Diagnosis of Pediatric Pneumonia Using Chest Radiographs
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of general-purpose LLMs on pediatric CXR classification
evidence.effect: Average diagnostic accuracy was 31%, consistent with chance-level performance in a three-choice task; concordance with human experts did not exceed 49% for any model.
evidence.quote: Across all models and CXR types, the average diagnostic accuracy was 31%, consistent with chance-level performance in a three-choice classification task.

evidence.title: Limitations of large language models in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on flexible clinical reasoning versus reported benchmark performance
evidence.effect: LLMs including o1, Gemini, Claude, and DeepSeek perform poorly compared to physicians on mARC-QA despite human-level accuracy on medical QA benchmarks.
evidence.quote: We find that LLMs, including current state-of-the-art o1, Gemini, Claude, and DeepSeek models, perform poorly compared to physicians on mARC-QA, often demonstrating lack of commonsense medical reasoning and a propensity to hallucinate.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Performance and Fragility of Large Language Models on the Self-Assessment for Neurological Surgeons
evidence.outcome: Whether exam-style benchmark performance reflects robustness in realistic clinical text
evidence.effect: 6 of 28 LLMs passed the board threshold, but performance was markedly vulnerable to extraneous distracting information.
evidence.quote: While current LLMs demonstrate an impressive ability to answer neurosurgery board-like examination questions, their performance is markedly vulnerable to extraneous, distracting information.

evidence.title: When Jack of All Trades Is a Master of None: Comparing the Performance of GPT-4 Omni against Specialised Neural Networks in Identifying Malignant Dermatological Lesions from Smartphone Images and Structured Clinical Data
evidence.outcome: GPT-4o triage performance for skin lesion malignancy
evidence.effect: Poor triage performance; balanced accuracy 0.571-0.622, sensitivity >0.95 but very low specificity.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity was consistently high (>0.95) with the trade-off of very low specificity.
evidence.sample_unit: random skin lesion cases from PAD-UFES-20 (50 repeated trials each)

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence for procedural coding in cardiac critical care: Evaluating large language models for current procedural terminology accuracy
evidence.outcome: CPT code accuracy of six LLMs on cardiac ICU procedures, ECMO vs non-ECMO
evidence.effect: Non-ECMO accuracy ranged from 56% (GPT-4.0) to 88% (Gemini 2.5 Pro, Perplexity). ECMO accuracy ranged from 0% (GPT-4.0) to 86% (Perplexity), with Claude 3.7 Sonnet at 14%.
evidence.quote: For ECMO-related codes, Perplexity outperformed all models (86%), followed by Gemini 2.5 Pro (71%), Mistral (43%), DeepSeek (29%), Claude 3.7 Sonnet (14%), and GPT 4.0 (0%).

evidence.title: A novel evaluation benchmark for medical LLMs illuminating safety and effectiveness in clinical domains
evidence.outcome: LLM performance on clinical safety and effectiveness benchmark, including high-risk scenarios
evidence.effect: Average total score 57.2%, safety 54.7%, effectiveness 62.3%; 13.3% performance drop in high-risk scenarios (p < 0.0001).
evidence.quote: Benchmark testing of six LLMs revealed moderate overall performance (average total score 57.2%, safety 54.7%, effectiveness 62.3%), with a significant 13.3% performance drop in high-risk scenarios (p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection and Subtype Classification on CT Imaging Using a Large Language Model
evidence.outcome: Zero-shot multimodal LLM accuracy for binary intracranial hemorrhage detection on CT scans
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy 0.52; recall 0.14 for hemorrhage-positive cases, 0.87 for negative cases; exact match accuracy 0.06 for subtype classification.
evidence.quote: For binary detection, the model achieved an overall accuracy of 0.52, with low recall for hemorrhage-positive cases (0.14) and higher recall for hemorrhage-negative cases (0.87).

evidence.title: [Study of the performances of conversational agents in interpreting textual description of lesions in pathology]
evidence.outcome: Domain-specific clinical competency of general-purpose LLM chatbots in pathology
evidence.effect: Response quality varied among the four chatbots; up to 82% correct diagnoses first attempt; quality correlated with online documentation volume per pathology.
evidence.quote: Out of 200 texts submitted, response quality varied among the four CAs, with up to 82% (ChatGPT) of correct diagnoses on the first attempt (91% after a follow-up prompt).

evidence.title: MedAlign: A Clinician-Generated Dataset for Instruction Following with Electronic Medical Records
evidence.venue: Proceedings of the ... AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence.outcome: Clinician-judged error rates of LLM responses to EHR instructions
evidence.effect: High error rates ranging from 35% (GPT-4) to 68% (MPT-7B-Instruct); 8.3% drop in accuracy for GPT-4 moving from 32k to 2k context lengths.
evidence.quote: We found high error rates, ranging from 35% (GPT-4) to 68% (MPT-7B-Instruct), and 8.3% drop in accuracy moving from 32k to 2k context lengths for GPT-4.
evidence.sample_unit: clinician-generated instructions for EHR data (303 with clinician reference responses; 276 longitudinal EHRs)

evidence.title: Accuracy Is Not Enough: Reasoning and Reference Reliability in Orthopaedic Large Language Model (LLM) Applications
evidence.outcome: Exam benchmark accuracy versus reference reliability of the model's supporting evidence
evidence.effect: GPT-5 scored 78.3% (159/203) on the OITE, but one in three answers cited fabricated or misrepresented evidence.
evidence.quote: GPT-5 appears to exceed previously reported LLM performance on the OITE and achieved accuracy higher than published mean scores for senior trainees, but demonstrated poor reference reliability, with one in three answers citing fabricated or misrepresented evidence.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large-Scale and Lightweight Large Language Models for Traditional Chinese Medicine Exam Questions: A Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on TCM exam questions by question type, model size, and prompt language
evidence.effect: Large-scale LLMs reached 69.01%-90.92% on single-choice but at most 8.40% on multiple-choice; evaluation was exam-style and not real-world clinical decision-making.
evidence.quote: While the current evaluation is based on examination-style tasks and does not involve real-world clinical decision-making, our findings provide insights to support the deployment of optimized models in resource-constrained healthcare environments.

evidence.title: A comparative accuracy study of multimodal LLMs, VLM and agent-based framework for pulmonary nodule detection on chest radiographs
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of multimodal LLMs detecting pulmonary nodules on chest radiographs
evidence.effect: Best accuracy 0.711 (95% CI 0.613-0.808) for MedRAX and BiomedCLIP; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 0.651; others 0.602. Accuracy insufficient for clinical implementation.
evidence.quote: Overall, accuracy values of evaluated models were insufficient for current clinical practice implementation.

evidence.title: Benchmark evaluation of video large language models in quality assessment of science popularization videos for dry eye
evidence.outcome: Agreement (ICC) between VideoLLM scores and expert ratings of dry eye video quality
evidence.effect: Across most metrics, VideoLLMs showed poor agreement with experts (ICC < 0.40); only PEMAT-A/V actionability reached ICC 0.50 (QwenVL) and 0.43 (InternVL).
evidence.quote: Across most metrics, VideoLLMs demonstrated poor agreement with expert annotations (ICC < 0.40), except for the actionability dimension of PEMAT-A/V, where QwenVL and InternVL achieved ICCs of 0.50 and 0.43, respectively, with the experts.

evidence.title: Assessing multimodal large language models for localizing dental implant fixtures on panoramic radiographs
evidence.outcome: Zero-shot localization performance of general-purpose multimodal LLMs on dental radiographs
evidence.effect: Micro sensitivity was 16.97% for GPT-4o, 68.82% for o3, and 65.66% for GPT-5T; specificity on implant-absent images 32.68%, 65.85%, 68.54%.
evidence.quote: Reasoning-focused multimodal LLMs outperformed GPT-4o in zero-shot implant fixture localization and reduced false positives, but moderate sensitivity, restoration-driven errors, and run-to-run variability limit autonomous clinical use.
evidence.sample_unit: panoramic radiographs (82 implant-present with 297 fixtures, 82 implant-absent), five runs each

evidence.title: Evaluating the Accuracy and Diagnostic Reasoning of Multimodal Large Language Models in Interpreting Neuroradiology Cases From RadioGraphics
evidence.outcome: Top-3 differential diagnosis accuracy of multimodal LLMs vs neuroradiologists on neuroradiology quiz cases
evidence.effect: LLM top-3 accuracy 29.9% to 49.4% versus radiologists 80.3% and 68.3% (P < 0.001); only 29.4% (118 of 401) of LLM analyses acceptable; hallucinations in 4.5% (18 of 401).
evidence.quote: Top-3 accuracy (i.e., correct answers present among top-3 differential diagnoses) of LLMs ranged from 29.9% (120 of 401) to 49.4% (198 of 401, obtained with GPT-4V in the T1 setting), while radiologists achieved 80.3% (322 of 401) and 68.3% (274 of 401), respectively (P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for clinical note processing: local fine-tuning and internal-external validation using electronic health records from South Asia
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Benchmark performance versus performance on real-world local clinical notes
evidence.effect: Models scored highly on public benchmarks (e.g., F1 0.83-0.96) but dropped on local notes (e.g., 3-label F1 0.58-0.71); benchmark-only evaluation is limited.
evidence.quote: These findings highlight the sensitivity of LLM performance to data distribution and underscore the limitations of relying solely on benchmark-based evaluations to assess real-world reliability.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical notes (50 discharge summaries, 150 SOAP notes)

evidence.title: Tests of large language models' medical competence and application for clinical decision support of musculoskeletal rehabilitation
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on musculoskeletal rehabilitation exam questions
evidence.effect: Only ERNIE Bot X1 Turbo and Doubao 1.5 pro exceeded 90% accuracy; other LLMs performed lower, so exam-style benchmark performance varied widely across models.
evidence.quote: In the first test, only ERNIE Bot X1 Turbo and Doubao 1.5 pro had accuracy rates of over 90%, and Chinese LLMs had significantly fewer incorrect questions than English LLMs (9.6% vs. 14.8%, P < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: LLMs tested on musculoskeletal rehabilitation exam questions and two clinical cases

evidence.title: Performance of next-generation AI chatbots in gynecological knowledge assessment: a comparative pilot study of ChatGPT-5, Gemini-3, DeepSeek-V3.2, and Claude-4.5-Opus
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on gynecology MCQs from USMLE-style questions under zero-shot constrained prompts
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy unsatisfactory: Gemini-3 32.86%, DeepSeek-V3.2 30.00%, ChatGPT-5 25.71%, Claude-4.5-Opus 21.43%; ChatGPT-5 scored 0.00% in Infertility.
evidence.quote: Contrary to expectations for advanced models, overall accuracy was unsatisfactory: Gemini-3 (32.86%), DeepSeek-V3.2 (30.00%), ChatGPT-5 (25.71%), and Claude-4.5-Opus (21.43%).

evidence.title: Automated Tumor International Classification of Diseases Coding of Real-World Pathology Reports Using Self-Hosted Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: LLM ICD-O-3 coding performance on real-world pathology reports versus need for deployment competence
evidence.effect: Best exact topography micro-F1 71.6% (Qwen3-235B-A22B); best exact morphology micro-F1 34.7% (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B); performance not sufficient for fully automated use.
evidence.quote: Although LLMs demonstrate promising capabilities as support systems for expert-guided pathology coding, their performance is not yet sufficient for fully automated, unsupervised use in routine clinical workflows.

evidence.title: MetaDent: Labeling Clinical Images for Vision-Language Models in Dentistry
evidence.outcome: VLM accuracy on intraoral image VQA, classification, and captioning benchmarks
evidence.effect: Even the most advanced VLMs achieved moderate accuracy (less than 70% in VQA) and produced inconsistent or incomplete image captions.
evidence.quote: Quantitative results reveal that even the most advanced models struggle with a fine-grained understanding of intraoral scenes, achieving moderate accuracy (e.g., less than 70% in VQA) and producing inconsistent or incomplete descriptions in image captioning.

evidence.title: Grounding large language models in clinical diagnostics
evidence.outcome: LLM performance on dynamic diagnostic workflows versus static tasks
evidence.effect: Existing LLMs proficient in static tasks fall short in dynamic diagnostic workflows and frequently commit clinical errors.
evidence.quote: Our evaluation shows that existing LLMs, including GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Claude-3-Haiku, Qwen2.5-72b, Qwen2.5-32b, and Qwen2.5-14b, while proficient in static tasks, fall short in dynamic diagnostic workflows and frequently commit clinical errors.

evidence.title: Assessment of Correctness, Content Omission, and Risk of Harm in Large Language Model Responses to Ophthalmology Continuing Medical Education Questions
evidence.outcome: Multiple choice accuracy versus prose reasoning quality of LLMs on ophthalmology CME questions
evidence.effect: MC accuracy 82.5% (99/120) ChatGPT-4 and 49.2% (59/120) Gemini Pro 1.5; prose showed incorrect reasoning (42%, 58%), missing content (42%, 30%), and possible harm (36%, 44%).
evidence.quote: Though there was high evidence of correct reasoning in the prose responses (92% and 88% for ChatGPT-4 and Gemini Pro 1.5, respectively), there was also evidence of incorrect reasoning (42% and 58%), inappropriate content (29% and 36%), missing content (42% and 30%), and possibility of physical or emotional harm (36% and 44%).

evidence.title: Benchmarking agreement between large language models and published clinical trial conclusions across four artificial intelligence platforms
evidence.outcome: LLM concordance with published clinical trial conclusions on benchmark RCT interpretation
evidence.effect: Concordance with published conclusions: ChatGPT 100.0%, Gemini 84%, Grok3 72%, Claude 68%; possible training-data contamination may inflate alignment.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT demonstrated the highest concordance with published conclusions at 100.0%, followed by Gemini at 84%, Grok3 at 72%, and Claude at 68%.
evidence.sample_unit: landmark RCTs (NEJM) interpreted by each of four LLMs

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence in Plastic Surgery Education: A Global Multimodel Benchmark of Large Language Models on the Plastic Surgery In-Service Training Examination
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on PSITE exam questions, as a proxy for clinical competence
evidence.effect: Claude Opus 4.5 90.2% and GPT-5.2 Pro 87.0%; proprietary mean 76.1% vs open-source 60.2%. Authors state accuracy alone is insufficient to judge clinical utility.
evidence.quote: Accuracy alone is insufficient to judge clinical utility; stability metrics are essential for selecting AI tools in surgical education.
evidence.sample_unit: model evaluations (14 LLMs x 100 questions x 5 runs)

evidence.title: Comparative performance analysis of AI-based large language models in assessing cervical vertebral maturation stages on lateral cephalometric radiographs
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy in classifying cervical vertebral maturation stage versus orthodontist consensus
evidence.effect: Exact-match accuracy 14% to 28%; within ±1 stage 55% to 64%; correlations ρ 0.3–0.616; wide limits of agreement.
evidence.quote: Current LLMs did not exhibit clinically acceptable agreement with expert CVM assessments, showing wide error margins that limit their clinical utility.

evidence.title: Performance of GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on the Orthopaedic In-Training Examination
evidence.outcome: Explanation validity and reasoning errors despite high exam accuracy
evidence.effect: Incorrect or partially correct explanations accompanied 45.4% of GPT-5 and 41.7% of Gemini responses despite accuracy of 76.0% and 81.1%, exceeding PGY-5 benchmarks.
evidence.quote: Incorrect or partially correct explanations accompanied 45.4% of GPT-5 and 41.7% of Gemini responses.

evidence.title: ChatGPT in a theoretical examination of Orthopaedic Surgery and Traumatology: clinical and educational value
evidence.venue: Revista espanola de cirugia ortopedica y traumatologia
evidence.outcome: Exam-question accuracy of general-purpose ChatGPT-4o versus residents, including image-based questions
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4o answered 34/48 (71%) correctly, above the resident average (67%), but only 30% accuracy on image-based clinical or radiological questions.
evidence.quote: However, its performance was notably lower in image-based clinical or radiological questions (30% accuracy).

evidence.title: The Performance of DeepSeek R1 and Gemini 3 in Complex Medical Scenarios: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Accuracy difference between closed-ended (cued) and open-ended formats on clinical vignettes
evidence.effect: DeepSeek R1 86.4% closed vs 80.9% open; Gemini 3 Pro 90.7% closed vs 88.9% open, showing benchmark format inflates accuracy.
evidence.quote: While the closed-ended format may inflate accuracy due to cueing, the open-ended evaluation yielded richer insights into the fidelity of reasoning.

evidence.title: AgentClinic: a multimodal benchmark for tool-using clinical AI agents
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy on MedQA problems in static format versus sequential agent format
evidence.effect: Diagnostic accuracies can drop to below a tenth of the original accuracy when MedQA problems are posed in the sequential decision-making format.
evidence.quote: We find that solving MedQA problems in the sequential decision-making format of AgentClinic is considerably more challenging, resulting in diagnostic accuracies that can drop to below a tenth of the original accuracy.

evidence.title: Clinical Context Variables Collectively Rival Model Choice in Embedding-Based Retrieval: Multi-Corpus Benchmark Study
evidence.outcome: Portability of general-domain model rankings to clinical retrieval tasks across corpora
evidence.effect: Model rankings shifted across corpora (model x corpus eta-squared=0.040, P<.001). Domain-specific BioBERT and ClinicalBERT performed worse than general-purpose embeddings.
evidence.quote: These results argue against reliance on general-domain leaderboards for clinical RAG deployment and support mandatory local validation as a methodological requirement.
evidence.sample_unit: documents (3 corpora x 500 documents each; 294 experimental conditions)

evidence.title: Performance of multimodal large language models for the detection and characterization of bone lesions on radiographs
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of general multimodal LLMs for bone lesion detection and characterization on radiographs
evidence.effect: Detection accuracy 0.803 for ChatGPT 5.2, 0.677 for MedGemma 4B; Claude and Gemini sensitivity 0.991/0.972 but specificity 0.038/0.201; DeepSeek-VL2 malignancy sensitivity 0.022.
evidence.quote: These findings suggest that, despite their potential, current multimodal LLMs are not yet sufficiently reliable for diagnostic use in orthopedic oncology and should be considered investigational until further development and validation.

evidence.title: Comparative analysis of generative pre-trained transformers for text- and image-based cephalometric prompts using a novel Artificial Intelligence Based Diagnosis and Treatment Planning Index (AIDTI)
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: GPT performance on cephalometric diagnosis and treatment planning (AIDTI 0-10) by prompt format
evidence.effect: Text-based prompts scored up to 9.62 ± 1.13 (GPT-5 pro); image-based prompts scored much lower, best 4.16 ± 4.12 (GPT-o3 pro). Models systematically classified malocclusions as Class II.
evidence.quote: By contrast, the performance of all GPTs on image-based prompts was notably lower, with the highest score being 4.16 ± 4.12 for GPT-o3 pro.
evidence.sample_unit: lateral cephalograms (30 each of skeletal Class I, II, III)

evidence.title: Humans vs. large language models in neurology board examination: performance, limitations, and reference reliability
evidence.outcome: LLM exam accuracy versus visual-question performance and reference reliability as competence indicators
evidence.effect: Accuracy 85-87% vs examinee 65%, but no advantage on visual items and high rates of fabricated or insufficient references.
evidence.quote: On visually based questions, accuracy was lower than for non-visual items, and the performance advantage over examinees disappeared.

evidence.title: Evaluating reasoning in multimodal large language models for ophthalmology: a bilingual benchmark study using clinical vignettes and imaging
evidence.outcome: Multimodal LLM accuracy and reasoning on ophthalmology vignette-plus-image benchmark questions
evidence.effect: Reasoning-enabled scores rose (e.g., ChatGPT-5 English 20.77 to 23.97; CLM-V Chinese 9.03 to 10.27), but limitations in subspecialty robustness and image interpretation remained; benefit was model- and dataset-dependent.
evidence.quote: However, limitations in subspecialty robustness and image interpretation necessitate rigorous reasoning evaluation for safe educational and clinical applications.

evidence.title: Head-to-head evaluation of ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Perplexity on acid-base disorder case clinical management and drug treatment: Accuracy, domain performance, and response consistency assessment
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on acid-base management and drug treatment MCQs
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy was 59.8% (305/510) ChatGPT, 58.8% (300/510) DeepSeek, 53.7% (274/510) Perplexity; only moderate performance.
evidence.quote: Overall accuracy was 59.8% (305/510) for ChatGPT, 58.8% (300/510) for DeepSeek, and 53.7% (274/510) for Perplexity (Cochran's Q p = 0.16); ChatGPT and DeepSeek each outperformed Perplexity (p = 0.0086 and p = 0.0374).

evidence.title: AI in respiratory care: findings from the GOLD report
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on 2025 GOLD COPD guideline questions, binary and open-ended
evidence.effect: Binary accuracy ranged from 89.5% (Gemini 3) to 97.1% (Kimi K1.5); binary error rates 2.9% to 10.5%; open-ended weighted-score deficits 3.5% to 8.2%.
evidence.quote: Residual performance gaps persisted across both domains, with binary error rates ranging from 2.9% (Kimi K1.5) to 10.5% (Gemini 3), and open-ended weighted-score deficits ranging from 3.5% (Gemini 3) to 8.2% (DeepSeek-V3.2).

evidence.title: The Effect of Structured Context on Chest Radiograph Interpretation by a Multimodal Large Language Model: A Pilot Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Multimodal LLM chest radiograph diagnostic accuracy against reference diagnoses
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy was 28% at baseline and 62% with structured context; lung cancer 20%, feeding tube placement 40%, rib fractures not identified in either condition; overall reliability inadequate for independent clinical use.
evidence.quote: Structured contextual guidance improved performance on selected chest radiograph tasks, but overall diagnostic reliability remained inadequate for independent clinical use.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Provide Accurate but Potentially Unsafe Answers to Multimodal Critical Care Medicine Board Review Questions
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT-4o on multimodal critical care board questions versus clinicians, and potential harm
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4o answered 74.9% correctly vs pooled clinicians 71.1% (p=0.03); image interpretation 61.7%, reasoning 68.3%; 33.3% of responses had potential for clinical harm.
evidence.quote: Notably, 33.3% of its responses were associated with potential for clinical harm, often due to incorrect image interpretation and treatment recommendations.

evidence.title: Performance of artificial intelligence chatbots compared with young academic urologists in reconstructive urology
evidence.outcome: AI chatbot scores on textbook MCQs versus urology experts; exam-style benchmark used
evidence.effect: Mean AI score 15/31 vs experts 14/31 (P=0.802); ChatGPT-4 24/31. Authors state use alone is unsuitable for clinical reasoning and needs validation on real clinical cases.
evidence.quote: These findings support a potential role for AI in educational settings and for answering well-defined theoretical questions, but their use alone is not suitable for clinical reasoning.
evidence.country: Europe (European Association of Urology YAU group)

evidence.title: Adherence of Artificial Intelligence Models to Brazilian guidelines for obesity in Primary Health Care
evidence.outcome: LLM adherence to Brazilian obesity guideline questions across diagnosis, monitoring, treatment
evidence.effect: Among 24 viable models, adherence was heterogeneous and limited, with the best performance reaching only 61.1% compliance.
evidence.quote: Among the 24 viable models, adherence was heterogeneous and limited, with the best performance reaching only 61.1% compliance.
evidence.sample_unit: LLMs evaluated on 16 guideline questions (of 62 screened)

evidence.title: From knowledge to judgment: A three-year longitudinal analysis of artificial intelligence large language model performance on the Chinese national nurse licensing examination
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on licensing exam: knowledge vs application sections, and clinical reasoning error share
evidence.effect: Average accuracy 81.6% on knowledge-oriented Professional Practice vs 70.9% on application-oriented Practical Skills; clinical reasoning failures were 43% of errors among top models; top accuracy 78.8% in 2025.
evidence.quote: Models exhibited superior performance in the knowledge-oriented Professional Practice section (81.6% average accuracy) versus the application-oriented Practical Skills section (70.9% average accuracy).

evidence.title: Benchmarking Zero-Shot Generative Pre-Trained Transformer-Based Multimodal Large Language Models for Pressure Injury Staging
evidence.outcome: Exact four-class pressure injury staging accuracy of zero-shot multimodal LLMs on public photographs
evidence.effect: Best exact four-class accuracy was 65.08% (GPT-5.2 structured JSON); Stage IV recall for GPT-5.2-pro was 8.79% (false-negative rate 91.21%).

evidence.title: Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts: evidence from BiasMedQA
evidence.outcome: Gap between public benchmark performance and performance on unpublished prompts (possible contamination)
evidence.effect: Gemini-2.5-Flash fell from 80.0-88.6% on public BiasMedQA prompts to 47.4-86.1% on unpublished prompts, hinting at training data contamination.
evidence.quote: The performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash dropped considerably when exposing it to four additional unpublished bias-inducing prompts (from 80.0-88.6% to 47.4-86.1%), hinting at potential contamination of its training data and exposing underlying brittleness.

commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-seven offline or benchmark-only studies suggest that exam-style scores and base-model results often diverge from how a specific deployed configuration performs on intended-use tasks, but none tests whether benchmarking the final configuration before deployment reduces patient harm. Evaluation teams can treat this recommendation as supported by regulatory expectation and consistent indirect evidence rather than by outcome data.

perspectives.view: All 27 tests are level 4 or 5 offline evaluations that compare models or formats. They show that task-based results differ from exam results. None compares deployments evaluated this way against deployments that were not, so the evidence is indirect. Designs, tasks, and metrics vary widely, which prevents pooling. Certainty is very low.

Results shifted with interaction format, model version, and fine-tuning. Triage accuracy rose 6.4 percentage points under naturalistic interaction, and three models scored 0 to 24% with forced choice but 100% with free text. A fine-tuned GPT-3.5 performed worse than its base. One study measured deferral and found it consistently expressed.

Several tests used non-English clinical data from Japan, China, South Korea, and Germany, and one used Nigerian health questions. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether deployment-representative benchmarks would detect performance gaps for these groups in health systems in the United States.

FDA draft guidance states that manufacturers must validate production units under actual or simulated use conditions for defined intended uses. The CDRH generative AI discussion paper asks manufacturers to evaluate the device for its specific intended use. The recommendation aligns with these expectations, although the discussion paper and the other endorsements are not binding rules.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares clinical outcomes, error rates, or adverse events between deployments that were benchmarked on intended-use tasks with local data and deployments that relied on exam or foundation-model results. Deferral behavior was measured in only one simulation. No study reports the staffing or cost of building deployment-representative test sets, and no prospective or real-deployment test of the practice exists.
commentary.underserved_note: Several tests used non-English clinical data from outside the United States, but none included Medicaid enrollees, safety-net patients, patients with limited English proficiency receiving care in the United States, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore cannot show whether this benchmarking practice would detect failures that fall disproportionately on those patients. Local test sets would need to deliberately include them.
